**Summary.** The paper presents an all-optical platform for controlling Coherent Perfect Absorption (CPA) by utilizing frequency conversion within a lithium niobate waveguide. By coupling the signal field's loss channel to a non-resonant environmental mode, the system achieves tunable absorption up to 92%. Furthermore, injecting light into this environmental mode allows for active enhancement or suppression of the absorption process.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it demonstrates a method for actively controlling dissipation in optical systems using nonlinear optics, which has parallels to engineered loss channels studied in open quantum systems theory and cavity QED.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to achieve all-optically controllable Coherent Perfect Absorption (CPA), overcoming the limitation of conventional CPA which relies on fixed material loss.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated a frequency-conversion-based platform where absorption can be controlled by tuning the pump light and injecting an external environmental field, achieving up to 92% absorption.

**Method.** The experiment uses a periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide resonator placed in a cavity to induce effective loss via nonlinear frequency conversion from a signal beam to an environmental mode.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled as a two-port beamsplitter coupled through frequency conversion. The control mechanism involves coupling the resonant signal field ($\lambda = 1581 	ext{ nm}$) to a non-resonant environmental mode ($\lambda_e = 780 	ext{ nm}$) using a pump beam ($\lambda_p = 1540 	ext{ nm}$).

**Key observables.** Transmission, reflection, and converted-light spectra; absorption efficiency (up to 92%); dependence of absorption on relative phase between counterpropagating signals.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Pump power, environmental field amplitude ($\alpha_{e,	ext{in}}$), cavity detuning ($\Delta_c$), and coupling constants.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis treats fields as classical complex amplitudes; for initial derivations, internal loss was assumed zero.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the concept diagram (Fig. 1) and experimental setup (Fig. 2). Subsequent figures show pump-power dependence of output spectra (Fig. 3, 4), high absorption with two-sided input (Fig. 5), phase control (Fig. 6), and enhancement/suppression via environmental injection (Fig. 7).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the concept of FC-CPA using frequency conversion to demonstrate tunable loss, then details measurements showing high absorption with two-sided input, and finally extends the model to show active control (enhancement/suppression) by injecting an external environmental field.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Coherent perfect absorption (CPA) extinguishes optical fields through interference and dissipation, but conventional implementations rely on material loss that is largely fixed after fabrication. Here we demonstrate all-optically controllable CPA based on frequency conversion in a periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide resonator. Pump-driven frequency conversion couples a resonant signal field at 1581 nm in the main system to a non-resonant environmental mode at 780 nm, creating a dynamically tunable effective loss channel. The nonlinear cavity acts as a tunable lossy beamsplitter without intrinsic material absorption. Under coherent two-sided signal injection, we observe up to 92 % absorption. We further introduce environment-assisted CPA by injecting an external field into the frequency-converted environmental mode, turning the environment from a passive loss reservoir into an addressable coherent control port. Our results establish a frequency-conversion-based platform for all-optical control of dissipation in CPA, combining pump-tunable loss with environment-assisted coherent control.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper uses the solvable Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model to study how measuring only part of a quantum system forces the remaining degrees of freedom into a statistically predictable state called the Scrooge ensemble. By mapping the problem onto path integrals and applying large-N techniques, the authors analytically prove that this emergence occurs even at very short times, establishing a key theoretical benchmark for understanding quantum measurement statistics.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between quantum measurements, deep thermalization, and universal random ensembles (Scrooge) is highly relevant for understanding information scrambling in strongly interacting quantum systems, which is a core topic in modern condensed matter theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the statistical structure of post-measurement states when only a subsystem of a quantum system is measured, leading to the concept of deep thermalization.

**Main result.** The moments of the projected ensemble are shown to exactly match those of the Scrooge ensemble, confirming that the SYK model provides a tractable setting for studying this universal statistical behavior.

**Method.** The analysis employs path integrals and large-N expansions applied to the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model to analytically characterize the moments of the projected states.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by the solvable Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) Hamiltonian acting on Majorana fermions. The procedure involves initializing in a Thermofield Double state, evolving unitarily, and then performing projective measurements on one subsystem.

**Key observables.** Measurement probability ($p_m$), projected ensemble ($\{p_m, |\psi_mangle_A\}$), Shannon participation entropy ($S_1/N$), and the first moment of the reduced density matrix ($ho_A$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Evolution time ($t$), system size ($N$), and coupling strength ($J$). The analysis explores limits like $N 	o \infty$ and short evolution times.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculation relies on the large-N limit, self-averaging properties of the SYK partition function, and assumptions regarding positive fermion parity for post-measurement states.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the schematic setup involving TFD state initialization and measurement (Fig. 1). Other figures show path-integral representations for probabilities and density matrices (Fig. 2), and numerical results tracking probability distributions and entropy as a function of time (Fig. 3).

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the formalism by first setting up the path integral representation for measurement processes in the SYK model, deriving saddle-point equations for the partition functions ($Z_m$), and finally calculating observables like the participation entropy and the reduced density matrix ($ho_A$) to confirm agreement with the Scrooge ensemble statistics.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The probabilistic nature of quantum measurement provides a direct window into the structure and complexity of many-body wave functions. When only part of a system is measured, the remaining degrees of freedom form an ensemble of post-measurement states whose statistical structure can reveal a stronger form of thermalization, known as deep thermalization. Recent numerical evidence suggests that this phenomenon is characterized by convergence of the projected ensemble to the Scrooge ensemble, a maximally random ensemble compatible with a given density matrix. In this Letter, we use the solvable Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model to unveil the mechanism by which the Scrooge ensemble emerges in many-body systems. By formulating measurement probabilities and post-measurement states in terms of path integrals, we analytically characterize all moments of the projected ensemble and show that they exactly match those of the Scrooge ensemble, even at short evolution times. We further connect this result to the saddle-point structure of the measurement path integral, which naturally generates the replica permutations underlying Scrooge statistics. Our results establish the solvable SYK model as a tractable setting for exploring universal statistics of quantum measurements in chaotic many-body dynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper investigates whether coupling a local probe qubit to a small, programmable bath can mimic the behavior of an infinite canonical bath. By measuring diagnostics like sector memory variance ($M_N$) and Gibbs-fit error ($\Delta_{	ext{global}}^G$), the authors show that finite environments only achieve local equilibration within conserved sectors, failing to erase preparation-dependent 'sector memory'.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, experimentally testable criterion for 'bath emergence' in engineered quantum systems, moving beyond idealized assumptions to address finite-size effects crucial for realistic open quantum system modeling.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to distinguish if a finite quantum environment acts as a true canonical bath, which would lead to preparation-independent probe states, or if it only causes local equilibration within constrained sectors due to conservation laws.

**Main result.** The authors conclude that equilibration within constrained sectors is insufficient to produce a single sector-independent Gibbs state, demonstrating a persistent 'sector memory' obstruction.

**Method.** They use theoretical analysis of infinite-time averages combined with experimental implementation on superconducting qubits using charge-preserving Floquet circuits.

**Model / system.** The system consists of a probe qubit coupled to a finite programmable bath of N qubits, governed by an excitation-number-conserving Hamiltonian. The dynamics are analyzed via sector-resolved time averaging.

**Key observables.** Sector-memory variance ($M_N$) and Global Gibbs-fit error ($\Delta_{	ext{global}}^G$); these quantify the deviation from a single canonical state description across different charge sectors.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The bath size (N), circuit depth, and symmetry-breaking strength ($\epsilon$) are key parameters varied in the analysis.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The conclusion is operational and limited to finite circuit depths; the diagnostics rely on analyzing time averages within conserved charge sectors.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate paired symmetry-breaking scans showing how perturbations reduce diagnostic errors but fail to eliminate sector ordering, confirming persistent memory effects.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical framework using conserved charges and defines diagnostics ($M_N$, $\Delta_{	ext{global}}^G$). It then presents exact simulations and validates these concepts on an IBM Fez hardware platform through controlled circuit implementations and disorder scans.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Finite quantum environments can relax local probes without acting as canonical baths. We study this distinction for a probe qubit coupled to a programmable bath of ($N$) qubits under excitation-number-conserving dynamics. The conserved charge partitions the Hilbert space into sectors. We characterize probe-level bath emergence using the sector-resolved late-time population ($p_e^{(q)}$), the sector-memory variance ($M_N$), and a global Gibbs-fit error ($Δ_G^{\mathrm{global}}$). Exact simulations with Haar-random pure states in each complete fixed-charge sector yield sector-dependent populations close to the maximally mixed-sector benchmark ($p_e^{(q)}=q/(N+1)$), producing a nonzero Gibbs obstruction. We then construct charge-preserving Floquet circuits using ($R_z$) phases and ($XX+YY$) exchange gates, validate them with ideal and noisy Qiskit simulations, and implement finite-depth experiments on IBM Fez. For ($N=4$) and ($ε=0$), the hardware data give ($M_N \simeq 0.044$), ($Δ_G^{\mathrm{global}} \simeq 0.558$), and charge preservation near 0.90 after readout mitigation. A paired symmetry-breaking scan using bath ($R_x(ε)$) rotations reduces both diagnostics while increasing charge leakage, but does not erase sector ordering over the accessible depths. These results show that equilibration within constrained sectors is insufficient to produce a single sector-independent Gibbs state for the probe.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes using coherent laser fields to actively control the rate of energy transfer between donor and acceptor molecules in a system immersed in thermal noise. By exploiting quantum interference effects, researchers demonstrate that the energy flux can be switched or enhanced simply by tuning the relative phase of the driving lasers, proving robust control in a realistic, dissipative environment.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it extends quantum control concepts from idealized transient dynamics into realistic, noisy, non-equilibrium steady states characteristic of biological energy conversion processes at ambient temperatures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research addresses the coherent control of energy transport within a non-equilibrium steady state (NESS) in a system coupled to a noisy, dissipative environment at room temperature.

**Main result.** Coherent excitation can induce interference between energy transfer pathways, allowing for phase-dependent modulation—acting as an optical energy switch—even when the system is operating in a highly dissipative regime.

**Method.** The analysis involves solving the master equation to find the NESS, utilizing theoretical frameworks like the Redfield and Lindblad approaches to model open quantum dynamics.

**Model / system.** The model is a minimal donor-acceptor pair connected to a reaction center, treated as an open quantum system interacting with both incoherent radiation (pumping) and a phonon bath. The evolution is governed by a master equation incorporating various coupling terms.

**Key observables.** Energy flux ($F$) between the donor and acceptor sites; Donor-acceptor coherence ($	ilde{ho}_{ad}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Relative phase ($\phi$) of coherent fields, bath temperature (300 K), reorganization energy ($\lambda_b$), and coupling ratios ($\Omega/J(\Gamma)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the Markovian approximation and weak system-bath coupling. For NESS calculations, analytical solutions are often intractable, necessitating numerical methods.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate flux modulation as a function of relative phase ($\phi$) for different pumping conditions, and show how the calculated flux depends on the ratio between coherent field strength ($\Omega$) and bath spectral density ($J(\Gamma)$).

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from defining the full Hamiltonian and master equation to deriving simplified Liouvillians (system-bath and system-radiation) under approximations. It then analyzes the steady-state flux in different coupling regimes, culminating in demonstrating phase control.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Coherent control of energy transport in a non-equilibrium steady-state (NESS) in a reaction-center-connected donor-acceptor pair is proposed. The pigments are considered to be continuously interacting with incoherent radiation and a phonon bath while being driven by phase-controlled coherent fields. Coherent excitation of the donor-acceptor pair is shown to induce interference between excitation pathways, resulting in phase dependent modulation of the flux. As a consequence one can enhance or suppress energy transfer via interference, e.g. an optical energy switch. The persistence of such interference enables coherent control at a NESS in dissipative regime suggests an extension of the operational scope of quantum control from traditional transient domain with low dissiaption to noisy environment NESS at room temperature.

</details>

**Summary.** The research reports the creation of an integrated platform combining neutral-atom arrays with a high-finesse Fabry-Pérot cavity. By developing novel mirror fabrication techniques, they achieved strong single-atom coupling ($\eta_{	ext{cav}} \approx 125$) while maintaining the large mode volume necessary for trapping many atoms. This opens pathways for complex quantum simulations involving collective atomic interactions mediated by light.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses a major engineering hurdle in quantum simulation: creating large, controllable arrays of qubits (atoms) that are strongly coupled to high-quality optical cavities for advanced quantum state manipulation and entanglement generation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge is integrating neutral-atom arrays, which offer scalable qubit architectures, with high-cooperativity optical cavities, which provide strong light-matter coupling.

**Main result.** The authors successfully realized an integrated platform achieving a single-atom cooperativity of $\eta_{	ext{cav}}=125\pm13$ while maintaining large mode volume compatible with trapping up to 16 individual atoms.

**Method.** They employed a two-step mirror fabrication process and characterized the system by measuring atom-cavity transmission spectra as the number of trapped atoms was varied.

**Model / system.** The platform consists of an atomic array (e.g., Rb-87) coupled to a millimeter-scale Fabry-Pérot cavity, enabling controlled interaction between individual atoms and the cavity mode.

**Key observables.** Single-atom cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{cav}}$), effective spectroscopic cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{spec}}$), and atom-cavity transmission spectra as a function of trapped atom number ($N$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** High cooperativity regime ($\eta \approx 100$), millimeter-scale cavity size, sub-2 Å mirror roughness, and the ability to couple up to 16 atoms simultaneously.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The difference between measured $\eta_{	ext{spec}}$ and theoretical $\eta_{	ext{cav}}$ is attributed to spatial spreading of atoms or placement errors within the lattice.

**Figures summary.** Figure 3 shows atom-cavity transmission spectra, demonstrating the measurable spectroscopic cooperativity ($\eta_{	ext{spec}}$) for varying numbers of trapped atoms ($N=1$ through $N=16$).

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the need to combine scalable atomic arrays with high-cooperativity cavities. It details the advanced hardware fabrication techniques, presents measurements confirming strong coupling ($\eta_{	ext{cav}}$), and finally demonstrates in-situ characterization by measuring $\eta_{	ext{spec}}$ across multiple trapped atoms.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Neutral-atom array and cavity quantum electrodynamics offer complementary strengths for quantum science: scalable, reconfigurable qubit architectures and strong coherent light-matter coupling. Combining them in a single platform requires an optical cavity with simultaneously high cooperativity, sufficient mode volume to accommodate atom array, and ample side optical access for atom trapping, imaging, cooling, and rearrangement, a combination that is challenging to achieve. Here we realize an atomic array integrated with a millimeter-scale Fabry--Pérot cavity whose optically-characterized single-atom cooperativity reaches $η_{\mathrm{cav}}=125\pm13$. Atom-cavity transmission spectra of trapped atoms yield an effective spectroscopic cooperativity $η_{\mathrm{spec}}=112.3\pm3.3$, providing an in-situ verification of strong coupling in the integrated platform, and we demonstrate simultaneous coupling of up to 16 individually trapped atoms to the antinode of the cavity mode. The key technical advance is a two-step mirror-fabrication method combining precision mechanical shaping and carbon-dioxide laser polishing, which produces concave fused-silica mirrors with sub-millimeter radii of curvature and residual roughness below 2 Å. Our results establish a regime of cavity-integrated atomic array that simultaneously provides high cooperativity, large mode volume, and flexible manipulation of individual atoms, opening opportunities for cavity-assisted quantum state readout and long-range entanglement-engineering in atom-array platforms.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a universal graph-theoretic framework to model open quantum dynamics by mapping the system's evolution onto two interconnected graphs. By applying this to the Open Quantum Rabi Model, the authors characterize how dissipation manifests as unique topological signatures within these graphs. This approach allows for efficient data-driven analysis and prediction of complex spectral properties using Graph Neural Networks.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, unifying mathematical language—graph theory—to analyze complex open quantum dynamics, bridging abstract topological concepts with concrete physical phenomena like dissipation and coupling regime transitions in cavity QED systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a universal graph-theoretic framework for mapping and analyzing both isolated and open quantum dynamics, specifically addressing the unexplored connectivity structure arising from system-bath coupling.

**Main result.** The authors successfully map open quantum dynamics onto two distinct graphs ($G_H$ and $G_L$), providing a rigorous mathematical tool to characterize dissipation signatures and enabling data-driven analysis via graph neural networks.

**Method.** The framework constructs Schrödinger operator graphs for the unitary part and uses a second graph derived from the Kossakowski matrix for the nonunitary (dissipative) evolution, allowing spectral analysis and machine learning prediction of Liouville spectra.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on open quantum systems governed by Markovian dynamics, exemplified by the Open Quantum Rabi Model (QRM), which includes coupling strengths ($\kappa, \gamma, \gamma_\phi$) and dissipation parameters.

**Key observables.** Liouville spectra ($\lambda$), graph-topological signatures of dissipation, Fiedler value ($\lambda_1$), and spectral distance measures like the Chamfer distance ($D$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coupling strengths ($\kappa, \gamma, \gamma_\phi$), pruning thresholds ($\chi$), and system size parameters ($N_{max}$). The analysis covers weak-to-ultrastrong coupling (USC) transitions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework relies on using the first standard form of the Lindblad QME to ensure all degrees of freedom are encoded in the graph structures, and it compares graph pruning against matrix sparsification techniques.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the constructed Schrödinger operator graphs ($G_H$ and $G_L$) for the open QRM under various coupling regimes. They show spectral comparisons using Liouville spectra ($\lambda$), demonstrating that graph pruning preserves spectral features better than direct matrix pruning, and present GCN training results.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the universal graph framework by defining two graphs ($G_H$ and $G_L$) representing unitary and nonunitary evolution. It applies this to the QRM, analyzing dissipation signatures and USC transitions using graph metrics. Finally, it develops and validates a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) trained on these graph representations to predict the Liouville spectrum.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Graph-theoretic frameworks have been widely employed in quantum physics to address the high-dimensional complexity of quantum systems. Although open quantum dynamics incorporates system-bath coupling via numerous interacting operators, it has been formulated algebraically with a partial set of jump operators or statistically universal reservoirs, leaving the underlying connectivity structure largely unexplored. Here, we propose a universal graph-theoretic framework for Markovian quantum dynamics. The framework maps open quantum dynamics onto two uniquely defined graphs, where the quantum master equation is rigorously interpreted as the average wave characteristic of operator-valued signals across the graphs. Applying this framework to the open quantum Rabi model, we demonstrate an open-system generalization of Fock-state lattices, characterize graph-topological signatures of dissipation, and classify the weak-to-ultrastrong coupling transition. Building on these representations, graph pruning reveals the backbone of open quantum dynamics, which enables superior graph neural-network learning. Our results bridge graph theory and open quantum dynamics, achieving efficient data-driven analysis of high-dimensional complexity.

</details>

**Summary.** The research demonstrates coherent quantum control of dark excitons—optically forbidden excited states—in MOChas at room temperature. By employing ultrafast pulse shaping and probing the system via Four-Wave Mixing, the authors show they can manipulate these states using a derived Hamiltonian model. This work establishes a solid-state platform for realizing fundamental quantum gate operations.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly bridges solid-state physics with quantum information science by showing how engineered excitonic states in organic semiconductors can be manipulated coherently using tailored light fields, mimicking atomic quantum control schemes.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The goal is to demonstrate coherent quantum control over dark exciton states within Metal-Organic Chalcogenolates (MOChas) for use in next-generation quantum processing platforms.

**Main result.** Coherent control was successfully demonstrated using ultrafast pulse shaping at room temperature, confirming the feasibility of using these solid-state systems for implementing basic quantum gate operations.

**Method.** The study combines theoretical modeling using a non-perturbative Hamiltonian with experimental techniques like Four-Wave Mixing (FWM) and ultrafast pulse shaping.

**Model / system.** The physical system is dark excitons in MOChas, modeled by a three-level system described by a two-photon Hamiltonian. The control mechanism relies on tailoring the spectral phase of an ultrafast laser pulse to manipulate state populations.

**Key observables.** FWM emission energy, which reveals resonance structure; the achievable quantum gate operations (e.g., $\pi/2$ rotation) characterized by pulse areas ($	heta$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Room temperature operation, two-photon absorption access, and the ability to tune detuning ($\delta(t)$) relative to coupling strengths ($\chi(t)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial theoretical description is limited to the perturbative regime, and the model simplifies by neglecting certain state couplings.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the excitonic state diagram (single-photon vs. two-photon allowed), the FWM experimental setup using a pulse shaper, and energy maps showing resonance features dependent on phase jumps.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical system and its limitations to developing a Hamiltonian description, demonstrating control via ultrafast spectroscopy measurements (FWM scans), and finally outlining the theoretical requirements for implementing quantum gates.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Artificial atom-like systems are a promising candidate for next generation quantum processing. Among them, dark excitons exhibit one of the longest lifetimes at high temperatures. Here, we demonstrate coherent control of dark excitonic states in metal-organic chalcogenolates (MOChas) by using an ultrafast pulse shaper at room temperature. These dark exciton states are optically accessed via two-photon absorption and directly read out with a four-wave mixing process. The system is described by a non-perturbative, two-photon Hamiltonian based on well-known atomic physics and applied to a three level system comprised of two dark excitons. Empirical and theoretical state specific optical access is shown via a simple optical pulse shape. The developed Hamiltonian-based description is a first step towards a quantum processing platform using three-level systems and two photon transitions, one example being dark excitons in the MOCha silver benzeneselenolate (mithrene). Simple conditions for gate operations are laid out and described.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper provides a comprehensive theoretical review of describing driven-dissipative quantum systems using the GKSL master equation. It argues that the choice of basis (e.g., diabatic vs. instantaneous eigenbasis) is critical, as it dictates the correct mathematical form of the evolution equations. By analyzing multiple bases for qubit and qudit systems, the authors provide necessary guidelines for theorists modeling complex open quantum dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it tackles a fundamental theoretical challenge: ensuring that the mathematical description of open quantum dynamics remains physically consistent regardless of the chosen computational basis, which is crucial for accurate modeling in quantum optics and superconducting circuits.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is determining the correct mathematical basis for formulating the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equation when describing driven-dissipative quantum systems.

**Main result.** The choice of basis—such as diabatic, instantaneous eigenbasis, or Floquet basis—fundamentally dictates the correct form of the master equation and its associated Hamiltonian terms, especially near avoided crossings.

**Method.** The authors analyze the GKSL equation by transforming operators and Hamiltonians between various bases (e.g., using transfer matrices) to ensure physical consistency across different dynamical regimes.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on driven-dissipative two- and multilevel quantum systems, exemplified initially by a qubit governed by a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(t)$. The dynamics are described by the GKSL master equation.

**Key observables.** Dynamics of the density matrix $ho$, stationary states (interferograms), and transition probabilities related to Landau-Zener tunneling.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Driving parameters ($\Delta, \epsilon(t)$), relaxation rates ($\Gamma_1, \Gamma_\phi$), and adiabaticity parameters ($\delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the Born, Markov, and secular approximations for deriving the master equation, and specific assumptions are made regarding the validity of basis transformations in different limits.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates energy level diagrams (diabatic, instantaneous, superadiabatic, Floquet) as a function of detuning $\epsilon_0$, while Table I summarizes properties of these various bases.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically revisits the GKSL equation derivation, analyzes its application to time-dependent Hamiltonians in multiple bases (diabatic vs. instantaneous), and discusses advanced techniques like superadiabatic and Floquet formulations for periodically driven systems.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

An open quantum system can be described by a master equation, of which one of the most popular is the Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) equation. We revisit description of driven-dissipative quantum systems focusing on the appropriate choice of the system's basis and the respective transformations. We consider the GKSL equation in different bases and calculate the dynamics for a qubit and for a qudit. An appropriate choice of the basis is a fundamental problem for theoretical consideration of open quantum systems and provides an opportunity to obtain the desired evolution in practice.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work characterizes the Dirac-Fermi Polaron (DFP), a unique quasiparticle formed when impurities interact with excitations near the Dirac point of materials like graphene. By calculating spectral functions and self-energies, the authors demonstrate that polaron spectroscopy provides a powerful tool to probe band structure effects beyond conventional measurements. The DFP is shown to be robust across various interaction strengths and doping levels.

**Why it may be interesting.** The focus on spectral signatures accessible in both solid-state (graphene) and ultracold atomic platforms makes this highly relevant for experimental quantum simulation groups working with strongly correlated systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how band structure effects influence the absorption spectra of quantum impurities embedded in Dirac materials.

**Main result.** They predict the existence of a robust, novel quasiparticle called the Dirac-Fermi Polaron (DFP), which is accessible via polaron spectroscopy even far from the Fermi surface.

**Method.** The analysis employs advanced theoretical techniques including the Loschmidt echo calculation and self-energy ($\Sigma$) methods derived from functional determinant approaches and variational ansatze.

**Model / system.** The model uses fermionic systems on effective honeycomb lattices, relevant to graphene, considering interactions ($U$) between impurities and bath fermions. The analysis covers both static and mobile impurity limits across varying doping levels.

**Key observables.** Absorption spectrum $A(\omega)$, quasiparticle residue ($Z$), polaron lifetime ($	au$), and the self-energy $\Sigma_{dd}(\omega)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interaction strength ($U/t$), chemical potential ($\mu$) relative to the Dirac point, and impurity mobility ($t_I$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on approximations like the Functional Determinant Approach (FDA) and variational ansatze for self-energy calculations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate absorption spectra showing AP, RP, and DFP resonances across doping levels; they also show the impurity spectral function ($\log$) and the calculated self-energy $\Sigma$ for both static and mobile impurities.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the basic polaron spectrum (AP, RP) to identifying the novel DFP at Dirac points. It then rigorously analyzes the DFP's robustness by incorporating impurity mobility and calculating quasiparticle properties ($Z, 	au$) via self-energy methods.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate band-structure effects on the absorption spectra of quantum impurities in Dirac materials. We uncover the formation of novel quasiparticles -- Dirac-Fermi polarons -- emerging from the dressing of impurities by excitations near the Dirac point. These quasiparticles are remarkably robust, persisting for both attractive and repulsive interactions, and across the full range of electron and hole doping. We show that their spectroscopic signature is a generic feature of Dirac materials, accessible with established techniques in both solid-state and ultracold atomic platforms. Our results establish polaron spectroscopy as a powerful probe of Dirac points at energies far from the Fermi surface, providing direct access to band-structure effects beyond conventional approaches.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces a novel method using a chirped Floquet linear drive to induce charge-to-spin conversion in Rashba 2DEGs along previously inaccessible directions. By breaking key symmetries like time-reversal symmetry, the chirp activates forbidden components of the spin Edelstein effect. This provides an experimentally tunable mechanism for advanced spintronic applications without needing external magnetic fields.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses open quantum systems dynamics by engineering time-periodic driving fields (Floquet engineering) to manipulate fundamental symmetries ($\mathcal{T}, C_{2z}$) in condensed matter systems, which is highly relevant for controlling spin-orbit torques and spintronics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is activating forbidden charge-to-spin conversion pathways (Edelstein effect) in Rashba 2DEGs beyond the conventional transverse plane.

**Main result.** A chirped Floquet linear drive successfully activates these forbidden spin Edelstein conversions by breaking rotational and time-reversal symmetries, offering a tunable spintronics route.

**Method.** The authors use Floquet theory to derive an effective Hamiltonian for the driven system and analyze symmetry properties of this effective model.

**Model / system.** The system is a Rashba two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) described by a specific Hamiltonian, which is then subjected to a time-dependent, chirped linear Floquet drive.

**Key observables.** Spin Edelstein susceptibility tensor ($\chi_{ij}$), quasi-energy bands, and the components of the effective Hamiltonian ($h_0, h_x, h_y$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Chirp parameter ($c$), harmonic order ($n$), Rashba coupling strength ($\alpha$), and low temperature limit ($k_B T = 1 	ext{ meV}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Calculations utilize the Kubo formula within the relaxation-time approximation, and the analysis relies on Floquet expansion techniques.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the activation of longitudinal/out-of-plane spin components via the chirped drive, show quasi-energy band structures, and map out the dependence of responses on chirp parameters and polarization angles.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the physical limitation (transverse confinement) to proposing the chirped drive solution. It details the derivation of the effective Hamiltonian using Floquet theory, analyzes how symmetry breaking enables new terms in the susceptibility tensor, and concludes with experimental accessibility via optical modulators.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In Rashba two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs), charge-to-spin conversion via the Edelstein effect is conventionally limited to the transverse plane. Accessing longitudinal or out-of-plane pathways typically requires static magnetic fields or interface engineering, which cause stray fields and lack tunability. While dynamic circular or elliptical Floquet drives can also unlock these forbidden pathways, a simple Floquet linear drive cannot. Here, we propose an alternative approach: a \textit{chirped} Floquet linear drive. The chirp induces in-plane Floquet-Zeeman fields and an odd-parity momentum drift, which simultaneously break rotational and time-reversal symmetries. This mechanism activates the forbidden Edelstein charge-to-spin conversions in Rashba 2DEGs. Experimentally accessible via programmable spatial light modulators or optical delay lines, this tunable chirped linear drive offers a broadly applicable route to spin-orbit torque switching and high-efficiency spintronics.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a dynamic theory for superconductivity in unconventional materials by treating the superconducting pair field as having memory effects due to local electronic fluctuations. It unifies spectroscopic measurements like ARPES and Raman scattering into a single framework governed by Gaussian-memory parabolic-cylinder functions, providing a detailed picture of how spectral weight shifts across different energy scales during the superconducting transition.

**Why it may be interesting.** The use of memory effects derived from statistical ensembles to describe phase transitions is highly relevant to open quantum systems dynamics. The connection between spectral weight redistribution and structured decay envelopes provides a powerful tool for analyzing complex many-body relaxation processes.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To develop a dynamical description of the superconducting pair field that treats it as a memory-dressed Bogoliubov pair field, moving beyond static order parameter approximations.

**Main result.** The superconducting transition reorganizes spectral weight between an incoherent pseudogap memory channel and a coherent condensate-assisted Bogoliubov memory channel. The response is unified by a Gaussian-memory Parabolic-Cylinder Function (PCF) framework.

**Method.** The authors derive the dynamics by coupling the pair field to fluctuating local modes, leading to an ensemble average that introduces a characteristic Gaussian memory factor into the effective action.

**Model / system.** The model focuses on unconventional superconductors, specifically cuprates like Bi2Sr2CaCu2O(8+d). The theory uses the Cooper-channel Hubbard-Stratonovich field ($\Delta$) and incorporates fluctuations arising from momentum-space spectral cavities (the pseudogap).

**Key observables.** Frequency-domain response expressed via parabolic-cylinder functions; measurable quantities include Raman spectra, ARPES background signatures, and superconducting gap features.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Critical temperatures ($T^*$, $T_{	ext{pair}}$, $T_c$); characteristic dephasing times ($	au_{	ext{pg}}, 	au_{	ext{sc}}$); algebraic power laws ($p=-1/2, 1/2, 1, \dots$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The ensemble averaging of local frequency shifts is approximated as Gaussian to yield the exponential memory factor. The framework assumes that different spectroscopic probes are projections of a single underlying PCF continuum.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the need for dynamic pair-field treatment, deriving the memory kernel via ensemble averaging over local fluctuations, and finally unifying the resulting spectral features (pseudogap, superconducting) within a single PCF mathematical structure.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We develop a dynamical description of the superconducting pair field in which the Cooper-channel Hubbard--Stratonovich field $Δ$ is treated as a memory-dressed Bogoliubov pair field rather than as a purely static order parameter. Starting from the standard pair-field effective action, we couple $Δ$ to antinode-selected collective or self-generated fields. An ensemble of such modes produces a distribution of local Bogoliubov frequencies; when this distribution is approximately Gaussian, ensemble averaging gives the memory factor $\exp[-t^2/(2τ_g^2)]$. In cuprate superconductors, the antinodal gap or pseudogap restricts the active electronic phase space and acts as a momentum-space spectral cavity. It selects fluctuation wavevectors $\mathbf Q_a$ that may become charge-density-wave-like instabilities in an ordered limit, but behave as a reservoir of local collective fields in the fluctuating regime. The same framework admits resonant algebraic prefactors, so that threshold and forced-oscillator responses generate the hierarchy $p=-1/2,1/2,1,3/2,\ldots$, while the Gaussian envelope cuts off secular growth and converts these branches into finite spectral components. The resulting picture contains a robust pseudogap memory channel and, below $T_c$, an additional condensate-assisted coherent channel proportional to $|Δ_0(T)|^2$. Thus the superconducting transition primarily reorganizes pair-field spectral weight between incoherent pseudogap memory and coherent Bogoliubov memory. The frequency-domain response is expressed in terms of parabolic-cylinder functions, and comparisons with Raman, ARPES, tunneling, and doping-dependent ARPES scaling suggest that these probes are complementary projections of the same Gaussian-memory pair continuum. We compare our numerical results with the recent experimental data on Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+δ}$.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reveals a previously unknown 'hidden gauge freedom' within the complex-pole HEOM formalism used for open quantum systems. By optimizing this gauge parameter, the authors introduce GO-HEOM, a method that significantly enhances numerical stability. This allows researchers to simulate strongly coupled or highly non-Markovian dynamics regimes that were previously inaccessible due to computational instabilities.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, general mathematical tool (the gauge optimization) to push the boundaries of numerically exact quantum dynamics simulations for open systems, which is crucial for modeling realistic quantum materials and environments.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is the numerical instability inherent in complex-pole Hierarchical Equations of Motion (HEOM) when simulating open quantum systems.

**Main result.** The authors discovered a hidden gauge freedom within the HEOM formulation, allowing them to construct GO-HEOM which eliminates spectral divergences and extends simulations into previously inaccessible strongly coupled or sub-Ohmic regimes.

**Method.** They analyze the structure of the Liouvillian generator by identifying a continuous gauge transformation parameter ($\phi$) that preserves physical dynamics while optimizing numerical stability metrics like non-normality.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on open quantum systems, using the spin-boson model as a primary benchmark. The theory is developed around the complex-pole decomposition of the bath correlation function $C(t)$.

**Key observables.** Time evolution of observables like $\langle\sigma_z(t)angle$, spectral divergence indicators, and non-normal error amplification metrics ($\eta_H$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Coupling strengths ($\alpha$), bath spectral density exponents ($s$ for sub-Ohmic), and the gauge-scaling parameter ($\phi_r$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The instability mechanisms (spectral divergence vs. non-normal amplification) are treated as distinct, controllable issues via the gauge transformation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison of dynamics using conventional HEOM versus GO-HEOM across various coupling regimes, demonstrating stability improvements and convergence with respect to the optimization parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the numerical instability problem in complex-pole HEOM. It then derives the existence of a gauge freedom ($\phi$) that parameterizes equivalent Liouvillians. Finally, it optimizes this gauge to create GO-HEOM and validates its superior performance across various non-Markovian spectral densities.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

While complex-pole hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) have dramatically expanded the reach of numerically exact quantum dynamics simulations of open quantum systems, they suffer from numerical instabilities rooted in the non-Hermitian structure of their Liouvillian. Yet, the origin of this structure remains obscure. Here, we report a previously unknown gauge freedom in complex-pole HEOM: a continuous family of analytically equivalent Liouvillians, all encoding the same bath correlation function, whose numerical properties vary dramatically. This gauge controls both the eigenspectrum and non-normality of the hierarchy generator, revealing spectral divergence and non-normal error amplification as two distinct instability mechanisms. By optimizing this gauge, we introduce GO--HEOM, which eliminates divergences in strongly coupled Brownian oscillator environments and extends numerically exact simulations of sub-Ohmic dynamics -- including through the delocalized-to-localized quantum phase transition -- to previously inaccessible coupling strengths. Because this gauge transformation is independent of the bath-correlation decomposition scheme, our GO--HEOM becomes a general, broadly compatible strategy for accessing numerically exact quantum dynamics of open quantum systems over arbitrary coupling and highly non-Markovian regimes.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically analyzes how nonlocality (Bell-nonlocality) can be shared sequentially among an infinite number of copies using incompatible measurements. It finds that this process leads to a unique 'Zeno-like confinement' where the resulting states converge while remaining nonlocal. The findings establish stringent constraints on measurement choices necessary for such robust, unbounded sharing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep theoretical understanding of how quantum correlations can be robustly distributed over many sequential steps, drawing parallels to physical phenomena like the Quantum Zeno Effect in open quantum systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research investigates the necessary conditions for sequentially sharing Bell-nonlocality among an unbounded number of copies using incompatible measurements.

**Main result.** Unbounded nonlocality sharing is possible, leading to a quantum Zeno-like confinement where successive post-processed states become almost identical while maintaining nonlocality.

**Method.** The authors analyze two measurement schemes (unsharp and PPM) by deriving recurrence relations for the post-processed state and imposing constraints based on the preservation of the Horodecki function ($H_k > 1$).

**Model / system.** The model involves a bipartite qubit system initialized in a nonlocal Bell diagonal state ($ho_0$), which undergoes repeated local measurements by sequential parties (Bobs).

**Key observables.** Violation of the Bell-CHSH inequality ($I_k > 2$) and the Horodecki function ($H_k > 1$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The asymptotic limit ($k 	o \infty$), measurement parameters (e.g., reversibility $q_{j,k}$ or strength $s'_{j,k}$), and initial state parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes non-adaptive measurements and focuses on pure strategies to maximize the nonlocality measure; the mechanism relies critically on one measurement being 'almost projective' (the anchor).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the requirements for unbounded sharing, derives post-processed states for two specific measurement types (Lüders/unsharp and PPM), analyzes the nonlocality preservation condition in the asymptotic limit, and constructs feasible sequences of measurement parameters demonstrating Zeno-like confinement.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

To enable sequential sharing of Bell-nonlocality by an unbounded number of copies, each copy must satisfy two requirements. First, the measurements must be incompatible to extract nonlocality. Second, the post-processsed state, obtained as an equal mixture of the two post-measurement states, must remain nonlocal. We show that the incompatibility requirements impose nontrivial constraints on the choice of the initial nonlocal state and the amount of measurement noise required to ensure that the post-processed state remains nonlocal for an unbounded number of copies. We establish this result for two measurement scenarios, namely, when each copy performs unsharp measurements corresponding to a pair of anti-commuting Pauli observables, and when each copy performs probabilistic projective measurements (PPMs) of a pair of anti-commuting Pauli observables. Furthermore, we show that, in the asymptotic limit, the nonlocal post-processed states of all the copies are almost identical, leading to a quantum Zeno-like confinement within the nonlocal region.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reinterprets infrared divergences (IRDs) as the physical signature of an 'itinerant vacuum'—a system continuously moving between distinct quantum states. Using advanced CTP formalism, the authors algebraically convert these divergences into a classical stochastic source term. This framework successfully unifies the origin of phenomena like $1/f$ noise and gravitational memory across diverse fields from QED to cosmology.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a powerful, non-perturbative tool for handling low-energy divergences in quantum field theory by mapping them onto observable classical noise sources, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems dynamics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper develops a constructive framework to interpret infrared divergences (IRDs) not as pathologies, but as signatures of an 'itinerant vacuum' undergoing continuous evolution.

**Main result.** It shows that the IRD can be algebraically converted into a classical stochastic source term within the real-time CTP effective action, unifying the origin of $1/f$ noise and gravitational memory effects.

**Method.** The core method involves using the closed-time-path (CTP) formalism and applying a Hubbard–Stratonovich identity to separate the divergent imaginary part of the influence functional into a classical stochastic source term.

**Model / system.** Applications include soft QED, scalar fields in de Sitter space, soft gravitons, and general non-equilibrium phase transitions, all modeled by evolving an order parameter through inequivalent quantum vacua.

**Key observables.** $1/f$ noise (in current or metric fluctuations), gravitational memory effects, and non-Gaussian fluctuations during phase transitions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dynamics are governed by the evolution of a classical order parameter across a manifold of vacuum states.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The approach requires no prior coarse graining or decoherence assumption; the stochastic source $\xi$ is treated as a c-number average because IR divergences do not depend on $\hbar$.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the concept of the itinerant vacuum, detailing the technical machinery using the CTP effective action and Hubbard–Stratonovich identity, and then applying this unified mechanism to several physical arenas (QED, de Sitter space, gravity).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Infrared divergences (IRDs) are usually treated as pathologies to be cancelled, regularized, or hidden in dressed asymptotic states. This paper develops a complementary and constructive viewpoint: an IRD is the signature of an \emph{itinerant vacuum} -- a quantum vacuum that wanders continuously through a family of inequivalent states as a classical order parameter evolves. Each value of the order parameter carries its own coherent vacuum, so moving the order parameter means traversing a succession of orthogonal vacua. The IRD is the field-theoretic cost of this wandering, and the $1/f$ noise, gravitational memory, and non-Gaussian fluctuations that emerge from it are its observable classical remnants.   The technical core is an exact separation in the real-time closed-time-path (CTP) effective action. The infrared-divergent imaginary part of the influence functional must not be left as a divergent coefficient in a deterministic equation of motion; it is instead converted, by a Hubbard--Stratonovich identity, into a classical stochastic source. This step is an algebraic identity of the generating functional and requires no prior coarse graining or decoherence assumption: the retarded kernel encodes the memory of past vacuum transitions, while the noise kernel encodes the quantum uncertainty of the next one. We apply this construction to four parallel arenas -- soft QED, scalar fields in de Sitter space, soft gravitons, and non-equilibrium phase transitions -- and show that the same itinerant-vacuum mechanism underlies $1/f$ current noise, the primordial power spectrum, gravitational memory, and order-parameter dynamics. A geometric formulation in terms of a Hilbert-space bundle over the vacuum manifold is outlined as an outlook.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper reports the deterministic generation of photonic cluster states in the telecom C-band using an InAs quantum dot. By leveraging hole spin qubits and characterizing the underlying process map, the authors demonstrated entanglement and achieved a three-qubit state fidelity of 0.71. This work is significant because it enables scalable quantum information processing compatible with existing optical fiber infrastructure.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses a major bottleneck in quantum networking by achieving high-fidelity photonic resource generation at telecom wavelengths using solid-state emitters, bridging fundamental physics research with practical quantum technology requirements.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to deterministically generate photonic cluster states directly within the telecom C-band, which is crucial for quantum communication compatibility with existing fiber infrastructure.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated deterministic generation of a three-qubit cluster state in the telecom C-band using an InAs quantum dot system. They achieved a process map fidelity of 0.71 and high photon indistinguishability ($\geq 83\%$).

**Method.** Cluster state generation is realized by implementing a Circuit Building Block (CBB) sequence involving controlled-NOT gates and single-qubit rotations, all characterized via quantum process tomography.

**Model / system.** The system uses an Indium-arsenide ($	ext{InAs}$) quantum dot embedded in a microcavity. Qubit encoding is achieved using the hole spin state, while photonic entanglement is generated through optical transitions to the positive trion ($	ext{X}^+$) at 1549 nm.

**Key observables.** Cluster state fidelity ($\mathcal{F} = 0.71 \pm 0.01$), spin–photon polarization entanglement negativity ($\mathcal{N} = 0.27 \pm 0.02$), and photon indistinguishability ($V_{HOM} \geq 0.83$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The process operates at an $80 	ext{ MHz}$ repetition rate, utilizing a hole-spin coherence time ($T_2^*$) of $15.9 \pm 1.7 	ext{ ns}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The characterization assumes that the fidelity can be extrapolated for larger cluster states by concatenating the CBB result multiple times.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the microcavity setup, the PL spectrum showing the $	ext{X}^+$ transition, and detailed circuit diagrams outlining the sequence of CNOT and single-qubit gates used to build the cluster state.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the physical platform (QD in a cavity), outlines the protocol based on CBBs derived from spin/photon interactions, presents characterization results via process tomography and entanglement measurements, and concludes with the demonstration of multi-qubit cluster state generation.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Photonic cluster states are a key resource for photonic quantum information processing. So far, deterministic generation of these states has been limited to the near-infrared wavelength range. To achieve quantum advantage in communication while maintaining compatibility with silicon photonics, operation in the telecom wavelength range is required. In this work, we demonstrate deterministic cluster state generation directly in the telecom C-band. This is achieved through repetitive excitation of a hole spin confined in an indium-arsenide quantum dot subjected to an external magnetic field. We characterize the quantum process that generates the cluster state by measuring its process map, obtaining a fidelity of $\mathrm{F} = 0.71 \pm 0.01$ to the ideal case. As part of this characterization, we observe spin--photon polarization entanglement with a negativity of $\mathrm{N} = 0.27 \pm 0.02$. The emitted photons exhibit indistinguishability of at least 83%, demonstrating the potential for future fusion gates necessary for photonic cluster state generation beyond linear connectivity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops the use of the normalized Wigner negativity rate as a diagnostic tool to probe the second moment of quantum wavepacket spreading in AdS$_3$. By analyzing this rate, the authors establish that it directly measures the rate of tidal stretching experienced by nearby infalling geodesics when the system dimension matches the critical Breitenlohner-Freedman value.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection between higher-order quantum measures (negativity) and classical gravitational dynamics (tidal forces/geodesics) provides a powerful, non-standard tool for testing holographic duality predictions.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research aims to move beyond first-moment diagnostics (like spread complexity) to probe higher moments of quantum dynamics, specifically using the normalized Wigner negativity rate.

**Main result.** The negativity rate matches the growth rate of the Krylov variance if and only if the dimension $\Delta$ equals 1, which corresponds physically to the rate of tidal stretching of infalling geodesics in AdS$_3$.

**Method.** The analysis employs techniques from quantum information theory (Wigner negativity) applied to dynamics generated by a local operator quench on a CFT dual to an AdS black hole.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled using the Krylov chain derived from a holographic CFT, whose evolution is governed by an effective Hamiltonian exhibiting $\mathfrak{su}(1, 1)$ symmetry. The statistics of the resulting occupation numbers follow a Negative Binomial Distribution.

**Key observables.** Normalized Wigner Negativity Rate, Spread Complexity ($\langle \hat{N}_{	ext{Krylov}} angle$), Krylov Variance, and the transverse string size operator $\hat{N}_{	ext{str}}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The conformal dimension $\Delta$, the time scale $t/eta$, and the Breitenlohner-Freedman dimension ($\Delta=1$) are crucial parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Key steps involve conjectures relating string operators to Krylov chain operators, and the analysis relies on specific asymptotic limits (macroscopic limit) and approximations for mode sums.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the inadequacy of first moments, then introducing the negativity rate as a second-moment probe. It develops the $\mathfrak{su}(1, 1)$ structure leading to Negative Binomial statistics, and finally connects this quantum diagnostic to geometric observables like tidal stretching in AdS$_3$.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In spread complexity, the average position of an operator along its Krylov chain, recovers the right radial momentum of an infalling particle in AdS, yet it is a measure of the first moment, irrespective of the spread of the wavepacket away from its classical trajectory. The rate of a normalized Krylov-Wigner negativity can be proposed as a diagnostic of the second moment of the boundary state that captures this spreading. Starting with the \emph{seed-normalized} Krylov-Wigner distribution -- that is, the Wigner transform of the descendant cloud, with the decaying return amplitude divided out -- we obtain an analytic Bessel form in the macroscopic limit and compute its total negativity explicitly. Retaining the Bessel variable all the way through, we find that the negativity goes as $\sinh^{4Δ}(πt/β)$, while the raw, seed-normalized state negativity saturates, as dictated by the $O(\sqrt{D})$ bound. Using the exact negative binomial statistics of the Krylov chain and the momentum dictionary of Caputa et al.~\cite{Caputa:2024}, the rate of the negativity scales as the growth rate of the Krylov variance at late time asymptotics \emph{if and only if} $Δ=1$, the Breitenlohner-Freedman saturating dimension in $AdS_3$. This dimensionality is special in that the negativity rate is the product of the proper radial position and momentum, $\mathcal{R} \propto \mathcal{C} P_ρ$, i.e., the rate of the tidal stretch of nearby geodesic falling into the horizon. We comment on the direction for future research, in particular the interpretation of the transverse string size operator in terms of the Krylov number operator through the common $SU(1,1)$ discrete series.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces the concept of 'irreducible degrees of freedom' (IDOF) derived from analyzing the bond algebra of quantum many-body systems. This IDOF count, $D_\lambda$, quantifies the thermalization capacity of a subspace, establishing a continuous hierarchy that smoothly interpolates between non-thermal scars and fully ergodic states. It provides an algebraic method to understand how local constraints dictate global thermal behavior.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful algebraic tool to quantify non-equilibrium dynamics, linking microscopic structure (bond algebra irreps) directly to macroscopic thermodynamic concepts like entanglement and ergodicity. It offers a systematic way to classify quantum scars within broader ergodic regimes.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To establish a quantitative 'thermalization hierarchy' that refines understanding of thermalization beyond simple symmetry sector decompositions in quantum many-body systems.

**Main result.** The thermalization capacity is controlled by the irreducible degrees of freedom (IDOF), quantified by the bond algebra irrep dimension ($D_\lambda$), establishing a continuous hierarchy from scars to ergodic states.

**Method.** Decomposition of the Hilbert space using the bond and commutant algebras, leading to an analysis based on irreducible representations ($	ext{irreps}$) and introducing the IDOF count as a diagnostic tool.

**Model / system.** The study uses SU(2)-symmetric spin-1/2 chains as a paradigmatic example. The framework analyzes how dynamics are constrained by algebraic structures derived from local interactions (bond algebra).

**Key observables.** Average eigenstate entanglement entropy, which is quantitatively related to $\log D_\lambda$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The bond irrep dimension ($D_\lambda$), which dictates the degree of thermalization; system size $L$ and total spin $S$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the algebraic decomposition provides a finer, physically relevant structure for dynamics than simple symmetry sector decompositions.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the thermalization hierarchy using diagonal blocks from the bond algebra decomposition. Other figures detail Young diagrams and specific mathematical decompositions of state amplitudes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically develops an algebraic framework by decomposing the Hilbert space via double-commutant pairs ($	ext{ASL}$ and $	ext{Asu}(2)$). It then applies this to analyze excitations (like two-magnon states) in terms of orthogonal components corresponding to different IDOF sectors, culminating in the definition of the thermalization hierarchy.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The decomposition of the Hilbert space of a quantum many-body system into the irreducible representations of its bond and commutant algebras yields a finer structure of dynamically isolated subspaces than the mere decomposition into symmetry sectors. While it has been recognized that subspaces associated with low bond-irrep dimensions $D_λ$ tend to violate the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), here we show that $D_λ$ controls thermalization continuously across the full spectrum of dynamical subspaces. Using SU(2)-symmetric spin-1/2 chains as a paradigmatic example, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{log} \ D_λ$ quantitatively accounts for the average eigenstate entanglement entropy within each sector, establishing a thermalization hierarchy that interpolates from exact quantum many-body scars at $D_λ=1$ to volume-law ergodic states at large $D_λ$. To make this concrete, we introduce the notion of irreducible degrees of freedom (IDOF), defined as the number of independently-varying spatial coordinates parametrizing a many-body state within a given bond-algebra sector, which provides a microscopic interpretation of $D_λ$ and of the resulting thermalization hierarchy. Finally, we show that by selectively breaking symmetries while preserving chosen bond-algebra sectors, one can embed families of nonthermal eigenstates at prescribed entanglement levels into an otherwise ergodic spectrum, generalizing restricted spectrum-generating algebras from towers of individual states to entire dynamical subspaces.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes how disentangling transformations reveal hidden symmetries in spin-1 quantum chains in the Haldane phase. By extending DMRG using Clifford circuits (CAMPS), the authors identify the optimal transformation as the Kramers--Wannier map. This mapping demonstrates a novel unitary pathway from topological order to symmetry breaking, providing powerful theoretical tools for characterizing quantum phases.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit connection between entanglement reduction techniques (DMRG/MPS) and fundamental physical symmetries ($\mathbb{Z}_2$ SSB) provides deep insight into the structure of topological order in quantum materials, which is highly relevant to AMO physics simulations.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the analytic structure of disentangling transformations used in simulating quantum many-body systems, specifically within the Haldane phase.

**Main result.** The optimal local Clifford disentangler for the Haldane phase is shown to implement the generalized Kramers--Wannier (KW) transformation, which maps the SPT phase to a state exhibiting spontaneous $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry breaking.

**Method.** The authors extend the Clifford-circuit-augmented Matrix Product States (CAMPS)-based Density-Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) method to spin-1 systems for analysis.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on spin-1 quantum chains, particularly those exhibiting the Haldane phase, modeled by Hamiltonians like the Heisenberg or Bilinear-biquadratic (BLBQ) chain. The analytically tractable state used is the Affleck–Kennedy–Lieb–Tasaki (AKLT) state.

**Key observables.** Entanglement entropy $E(\ell)$, ground-state energy error $\delta E_{GS}$, and long-range correlation functions $\langle S^z_j S^z_{j+r} \rangle$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis is sensitive to the specific Hamiltonian parameters (e.g., $D$ in Heisenberg, $\theta$ in BLBQ) and the bond dimension used in MPS representations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The core assumption is that the optimal disentangler can be found by optimizing over generalized Clifford circuits within the CAMPS framework.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare CAMPS-DMRG results for different spin models, showing energy error and entanglement entropy. Another figure compares correlation functions derived from KW vs KT transformations.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the CAMPS-DMRG framework for spin-1 systems; it then analytically proves that the optimal disentangler is the KW transformation; finally, it uses this transformation to diagnose a hidden $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry breaking mechanism distinct from other known transformations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Disentangling transformations play a central role in the classical simulation of quantum many-body systems, yet their analytic structure and underlying mechanism remain largely unexplored. Here, we study the structure of the disentangler in the Haldane phase of spin-1 systems using generalized Clifford circuits. To this end, we extend the Clifford-circuit-augmented matrix product states (CAMPS)-based density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method to spin-1 systems. Within this framework, we find that the local disentanglers optimized for the Haldane phase implement the generalized Kramers--Wannier (KW) transformation, and we analytically verify its optimality for the Affleck--Kennedy--Lieb--Tasaki (AKLT) state. Beyond reducing entanglement, the KW transformation maps the Haldane phase to a phase with spontaneously broken $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ symmetry. This mapping is distinct from the Kennedy--Tasaki transformation and provides a new unitary route from symmetry-protected topological order to symmetry breaking.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents a novel tensor network Variational Monte Carlo framework that drastically improves the scaling of simulating long-range interacting quantum systems from $O(N^3)$ to $O(N)$. This breakthrough allows for accurate classical simulation of complex dynamics, such as those found in dipolar XY models realized with Rydberg atoms. It establishes a powerful tool for benchmarking future quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a crucial computational tool—a scalable classical benchmark—for simulating complex quantum dynamics on emerging hardware platforms like Rydberg and ion traps, bridging theory with experimental feasibility.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing an efficient classical simulation method for two-dimensional quantum systems with long-range interactions, particularly those relevant to Rydberg arrays and ion traps.

**Main result.** The authors developed a tensor network VMC framework that reduces the computational cost of local energy evaluation from $O(N^3)$ to $O(N)$, enabling accurate simulation of previously intractable dynamics for systems like the dipolar XY model on a $10 	imes 10$ lattice.

**Method.** The core method is an efficient tensor-network time-dependent Variational Monte Carlo (tVMC) framework utilizing an adaptive basis approach to scale calculations from cubic to linear complexity with system size N.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on two-dimensional long-range interacting quantum systems, exemplified by the dipolar XY model ($H_{XY} \propto 1/r^3$) realized in Rydberg simulators. The simulation tracks time evolution under a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(t) = H_{XY} + H_Z(t)$.

**Key observables.** Local energy, sublattice magnetization (Z), nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor correlations ($C_x$, etc.), and squared staggered magnetization ($m_{2\alpha}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Long-range interaction decay ($\propto 1/r^3$), lattice size ($10 	imes 10$ for main results), and the time evolution parameter $\delta(t)$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The efficiency gain relies on an adaptive basis approach, which trades the zero-variance principle of fixed-basis VMC for computational tractability. For initial steps, Projected tVMC (p-tVMC) is used.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate benchmarks comparing TNS-tVMC results against exact solutions for small lattices ($4 	imes 4$), showing the time evolution of energy and correlations; larger simulations ($10 	imes 10$) confirm long-range correlation maintenance during adiabatic protocols.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of simulating long-range interactions, details the novel tensor network tVMC framework achieving $O(N)$ scaling via adaptive bases, applies this to simulate the adiabatic real-time protocol for a dipolar XY model in Rydberg arrays, and concludes by benchmarking its accuracy against known ground state limits.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In variational Monte Carlo (VMC) calculations of $N$-site quantum systems with arbitrary all-to-all two-body interactions, evaluating the local energy generally costs $O(N^3)$. We introduce a new framework that reduces this cost to $O(N)$ for tensor network states, capable of scalable and accurate computation of real-time dynamics and ground states. As a result, we obtain accurate simulations of the adiabatic real-time protocol of a $10\times10$ dipolar XY model realized in a Rydberg simulator [C. Chen et al., Nature 616, 691 (2023)], which was previously beyond the reach of classical simulation. Going beyond quantum experiments, we also directly perform ground state VMC to compare with the adiabatic state preparation. Our work demonstrates tensor network VMC as a powerful classical simulator for long-range quantum platforms such as Rydberg and ion-trap simulators, which are currently in urgent need of scalable classical benchmarking tools. As a separate technical contribution, we resolve the pathology of evolving from product states within of tensor network VMC.

</details>
