**Summary.** This work develops a graph-based Kirchhoff model to simulate electron transport in self-assembled nanonecklace networks exhibiting Coulomb blockade. By treating the network as a dynamic graph, the authors show that the characteristic non-Ohmic I–V response arises from voltage-driven percolation across threshold junctions. The framework allows independent tuning of structural parameters (density, topology) and electronic properties to engineer device behavior.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical circuit physics, the study's reliance on percolation theory in disordered media, threshold effects, and structural control parameters makes it relevant to understanding complex many-body dynamics in mesoscopic systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is understanding the poorly understood mechanisms governing the macroscopic non-Ohmic current–voltage (I–V) response in self-assembled nanonecklace networks.

**Main result.** The model successfully reproduces the power-law I–V behavior, showing that this nonlinearity emerges from the collective, staggered activation of threshold junctions and voltage-driven percolation.

**Method.** A novel graph-based Kirchhoff framework is developed to solve circuit laws on a dynamically changing conducting subgraph as bias is applied.

**Model / system.** The system models self-assembled gold nanonecklace networks as an undirected geometric graph. Junctions act as nodes with activation voltages, and segments are edges with length-dependent tunneling resistances.

**Key observables.** Non-Ohmic I–V response ($I \propto (V - V_T)^\zeta$), active nodes, conducting subgraph structure, nodal potentials, and edge currents.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Network density, structural topology (void fraction $f_v$), mean activation voltage ($\langle V_a angle$), and the spread of activation voltages ($\sigma_a$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model uses a simplified linear coupling for node resistance ($R_{n,i} = \alpha V_{a,i}$) and assumes global bias $V$ as the primary activation criterion.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the framework overview, step-by-step solver operation (Graph $ightarrow$ Subgraph $ightarrow$ Matrix $\mathbf{G}$), and parameter sweeps showing how density, void fraction, and voltage spread control transport exponents ($\zeta$) and threshold voltages ($V_T$).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the physical problem, details the graph-based Kirchhoff framework (including node/edge resistance models), presents simulation results demonstrating the emergence of non-Ohmic behavior from percolation, and concludes by establishing the model as a design tool for engineering transport.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Gold nanonecklace networks are promising platforms for single-electron switching, chemical sensing, and biogating devices because of their nonlinear current--voltage ($I$--$V$) characteristics arising from collective Coulomb-blockade transport. However, the mechanisms governing this macroscopic behavior remain poorly understood because experimental measurements are generally limited to the network topology and global $I$--$V$ response. To address this, we developed a graph-based Kirchhoff framework that represents a self-assembled nanonecklace network as a graph, with nodes corresponding to junctions between necklace segments and edges to the conducting segments themselves. The solver returns the active nodes, conducting subgraph, nodal potentials, and edge currents at each applied bias, while allowing the activation-voltage statistics, network density, and structural topology to be varied independently. The model reproduces the experimentally observed non-Ohmic response, $I \propto (V-V_T)^ζ$, and shows that this behavior emerges from the collective, staggered activation of threshold junctions and voltage-driven percolation of the conducting subgraph. Independent parameter sweeps reveal that the mean activation voltage shifts the threshold $V_T$ while leaving $ζ$ nearly unchanged, increasing network density raises $ζ$ from approximately 1.9 to 3.1 and enhances current, and topology controls the response even at fixed density and node characteristics. These trends agree qualitatively with experimental observations and establish the model as a design tool for engineering collective transport in self-assembled nanonecklace devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes using a superconductor/altermagnet/superconductor junction as a highly scalable, gate-controlled platform for parity-protected qubits. By exploiting the momentum-dependent spin splitting in altermagnets, researchers can electrically tune the Josephson coupling through a $0-\pi$ transition. This method eliminates flux noise sources and promises coherence times suitable for quantum computation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses a major bottleneck in superconducting quantum computing by proposing an all-electrical control mechanism that leverages novel magnetic materials (altermagnets) to engineer protected qubit states.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is developing superconducting qubits with long coherence times that eliminate the need for external magnetic-flux biasing, which introduces noise and limits scalability.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that using an altermagnetic Josephson junction allows for fully gate-controlled operation, achieving estimated coherence times up to tens of milliseconds while maintaining parity protection.

**Method.** The theoretical framework involves modeling the system Hamiltonian via a tight-binding approach and solving the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) equations to determine the Josephson potential and qubit energy spectrum.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is a superconducting qubit realized using an Altermagnet-Josephson Junction (SC–AM–SC). The altermagnets provide spin-dependent functionality without external fields, allowing electrical tuning of the junction's phase via chemical potential ($\mu$).

**Key observables.** Qubit splitting ($E_{01}$), coherence times ($T_1, T_2$), and the evolution of the Josephson potential through a $0-\pi$ transition.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gate-tunable chemical potential ($\mu$), offset charge ($n_g$), altermagnetic coupling strength ($M$), and charging energy ($E_c$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the low-energy limit of the AM region, assuming $M \ll t$ and $\Delta \ll \mu$, and initially focuses on the 1D geometry for simplification.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the physical setup controlled by gate voltages, the resulting double-well potential at the $0-\pi$ transition point, and the evolution of the Andreev bound-state spectrum and Josephson potential harmonics as a function of tuning parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem (flux noise), proposes the SC–AM–SC junction utilizing altermagnetism for electrical control, details the theoretical modeling using BdG/tight-binding methods to analyze the $0-\pi$ transition and resulting double-well potential, and finally calculates coherence times based on charge and chemical potential noise.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Parity-protected superconducting qubits offer intrinsically long coherence, but many current implementations require magnetic-flux biasing, which introduces flux noise, control overhead, and limited scalability. Here we propose a parity-protected qubit based on a gate-tunable superconductor-altermagnet-superconductor Josephson junction. Altermagnets are compensated magnets with momentum-dependent spin splitting and zero net magnetization, providing spin-dependent functionality without external magnetic fields. In the proposed junction, the two spin sectors acquire opposite phase shifts, generating two Josephson channels whose interference is controlled electrically by the chemical potential. At the tuned $0$-$π$ transition, the first Josephson harmonic is strongly suppressed while the second harmonic dominates, yielding a double-well potential with two nearly degenerate states of opposite Cooper-pair parity. For realistic gatemon-compatible parameters, we estimate coherence times of up to tens of milliseconds while maintaining fully gate-controlled qubit operations. These results establish altermagnetic Josephson junctions as a promising route toward protected superconducting qubits with local, scalable, and all-electrical control.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes how phonon scattering rules interact with boundary reflections in semiconductor nanofilms, leading to unique mode-polarized heat currents at low temperatures. By simulating these competing effects using first-principles methods, the authors show that this polarization allows for unprecedented control over phonon coupling compared to bulk materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on phonons (lattice vibrations), the concept of non-equilibrium energy transport and symmetry-selective coupling is relevant to understanding heat dissipation in quantum devices or open quantum systems where boundaries play a crucial role.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how phonon scattering selection rules compete with boundary mode conversion effects to modulate heat flow in nanoscale semiconductor films.

**Main result.** This competition leads to phonon mode-polarized heat currents, enabling symmetry-selective engineering of phonon coupling that is difficult to achieve in bulk solids.

**Method.** The study uses first-principles calculations solving the steady-state Peierls-Boltzmann equation (SSPBE) via a variance-reduced Monte Carlo approach.

**Model / system.** The physical system involves semiconductor nanofilms, specifically InP and BP, where heat transport is governed by phonon scattering mechanisms at cryogenic temperatures. The model explicitly accounts for intrinsic selection rules and extrinsic boundary reflections/mode conversions.

**Key observables.** Thermal conductivity ($\kappa$), phonon mode-polarized heat currents, LA and TA phonon contributions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cryogenic temperatures ($\le 100$ K), film thickness ($d$), material type (InP vs BP).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The Relaxation Time Approximation (RTA) is used; boundary conditions model conserving incoming/outgoing heat fluxes normal to adiabatic boundaries.

**Figures summary.** Figures show the dependence of thermal conductivity ($\kappa'$) on film thickness ($d$), comparing scenarios with and without mode conversion, and illustrate spectral contributions to $\kappa$ normalized by bulk values.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from established knowledge of phonon selection rules in bulk solids to model the competition between these rules and boundary mode conversion effects in thin films, culminating in predictions for engineered thermal properties.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Phonon scattering selection rules are known to control heat flow through bulk solids. Here we show that these selection rules also modulate heat flow through nanoscale semiconductor films, although through a previously-unexplored mechanism. Using first-principles calculations, we expose a competition between these selection rules and phonon mode conversion at boundaries of nanoscale films, that drives mode-polarized heat currents at cryogenic temperatures ($\le$ 100 K). This polarizing effect is stronger in materials like indium phosphide, where selection rules based on large velocity differences between phonon branches amplifies the longitudinal acoustic (LA) phonon contribution to thermal conductivity by restricting their intrinsic scattering events, while boundary mode conversion in nanoscale films suppresses it by depopulating the LA phonons. The resulting transverse-polarized non-equilibrium phonons will enable symmetry-selective engineering of phonon coupling to electrons, strains and defects in nanoscale films, that is difficult to achieve in bulk solids.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses micromagnetic simulations to map the interaction energy between a chiral bobber and a skyrmion string in a conical magnetic phase. The key finding is that this interaction is not merely distance-dependent but is strongly controlled by an intrinsic surface phase factor ($\phi_0$). This phase control dictates whether the interaction is repulsive, attractive, or leads to structural 'bonding' via shell reconstruction.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of an external 'phase factor' ($\phi_0$) acting as a primary control parameter for magnetic interactions is analogous to controlling boundary conditions or relative phases in quantum systems, suggesting new avenues for designing topological materials via field/geometry tuning.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the interaction between a chiral bobber and a skyrmion string, demonstrating that this interaction is fundamentally dependent on the local phase factor ($\phi_0$) within the conical magnetic background.

**Main result.** The interaction energy landscape cannot be described by a simple distance-dependent potential; instead, it exhibits distinct regimes (repulsive, attractive, bonding) controlled by $\phi_0$, which arises from structural reconstruction of outer spin shells.

**Method.** Three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations were used to compute the constrained energy landscape ($\Delta E$) as a function of separation ($R$) and phase factor ($\phi_0$).

**Model / system.** The system models magnetic films exhibiting bulk Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI), supporting topological spin textures like skyrmion strings and chiral bobbers in a conical background state.

**Key observables.** Interaction energy landscape $\Delta E(R, \phi_0)$, structural reconstruction of outer distortion shells, and the relative orientation parameter $\phi_0$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Separation $R$, surface phase factor $\phi_0$, magnetic field strength ($H$), and material parameters related to exchange/DMI.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Dipolar interactions were excluded from the primary calculations to isolate the minimal mechanism governed by exchange, bulk DMI, and Zeeman energy.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate contour maps of $\Delta E(R, \phi_0)$ showing three regimes (M, NM, Bonding); 1D cuts demonstrate repulsive/attractive sequences; and comparisons confirm top-bottom symmetry via phase transformation ($\phi_0 	o 180^\circ - \phi_0$).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical context of skyrmion interactions, develops the micromagnetic simulation framework to map $\Delta E(R, \phi_0)$, analyzes the resulting three distinct interaction regimes (M, NM, Bonding), and concludes by confirming the phase-factor dependence through symmetry relations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Skyrmion interactions govern the formation of skyrmion lattices, clusters, and particle-like growth patterns. In contrast, the interaction between a chiral bobber and a skyrmion string remains largely unexplored, despite the role of bobbers as intermediate states in skyrmion-string formation and annihilation. Here we show that this interaction is intrinsically phase dependent in the conical phase. Using three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations, we compute the locally relaxed constrained energy landscape as a function of the bobber--skyrmion separation $R$ and the surface phase factor $φ_0$. We find that changing $φ_0$ qualitatively reshapes the interaction, producing repulsive, attractive, and bonding-like regimes that cannot be reduced to a conventional distance-dependent potential. Real-space analysis shows that this behavior originates from phase-dependent reconstruction of nonaxisymmetric outer distortion shells. The phase-controlled interaction persists over a finite field range and follows the expected top--bottom phase relation of surface-sensitive conical textures. These results identify the conical phase direction, often hidden in projected or thickness-averaged descriptions, as a previously underappreciated degree of freedom in the interaction between skyrmion strings and finite-length chiral textures, as demonstrated here for chiral bobbers.

</details>

(2) (circles) and of a PB-type rank-two coupling of identical magnitude (squares): slopes 1 and 2, with no overlap at any integer q.</sub>

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel mechanism where light's spin can convert into orbital angular momentum (OAM) via material torsion, yielding the selection rule $\Delta\ell=q$. This contrasts sharply with the standard Pancharatnam–Berry effect ($\Delta\ell=2q$). The authors confirm this theoretically and propose an experiment using patterned photonic lattices to measure this distinct signature.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a clean, geometrically derived physical mechanism for light-matter interaction that deviates from standard optical models, offering a new platform to probe fundamental concepts like geometric torsion in photonics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to distinguish between two mechanisms for converting light's spin angular momentum (SAM) into orbital angular momentum (OAM): the standard Pancharatnam–Berry (PB) mechanism and a novel process mediated by geometric torsion.

**Main result.** Torsion predicts a selection rule $\Delta\ell=q$, which is distinct from the PB prediction of $\Delta\ell=2q$. This difference can be experimentally verified using polarization-resolved photonic lattice discriminators.

**Method.** The authors use paraxial simulations to confirm the theoretical selection rules and propose an experimental setup involving femtosecond-written photonic lattices for measurement.

**Model / system.** The system involves light propagating through a medium exhibiting geometric torsion, modeled using Riemann–Cartan geometry. The dynamics are governed by an effective paraxial Maxwell model coupling circular polarization to spatial structure via contortion and torsional phase rates.

**Key observables.** The ratio of measured OAM ($\ell$) versus the independently written texture charge ($q$); sideband positions showing slopes of 1 (torsion) vs. 2 (PB).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Texture charge $q$, conversion efficiency $\eta \approx 83\%$, and the topological quantization of the resulting vortex ($\ell=+q$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes the coupling is linear in the written contortion vector for the proposed experiment, and it contrasts the torsion mechanism with the standard PB director formalism.

**Figures summary.** Figure 3 predicts that OAM vs. texture charge plots will show non-overlapping sidebands: $\Delta\ell=q$ for torsion and $\Delta\ell=2q$ for PB coupling.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical difference in selection rules ($\Delta\ell=2q$ vs. $\Delta\ell=q$) based on the underlying geometry (director vs. contortion). It then presents paraxial simulations confirming the torsional rule and concludes by proposing a concrete, polarization-resolved discriminator experiment.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Standard Pancharatnam-Berry and linear-birefringent media convert optical spin into orbital angular momentum (OAM) through an anisotropy \emph{director}, a rank-two, headless field, and therefore obey the selection rule $Δ\ell=2q$ per unit texture charge $q$. We show that a medium with geometric \emph{torsion}, the continuum limit of a screw-dislocation array, can convert spin to OAM through the \emph{contortion} of its material connection, which enters the effective paraxial dynamics as a rank-one vector field. The resulting selection rule is $Δ\ell=q$. Its winding is fixed by geometry and symmetry, not by a Pancharatnam--Berry director, and the process conserves the screw charge $\tilde J_z=L_z+(q/2)σ_z$ while exchanging $(2-q)\hbar$ of angular momentum per converted photon with the defect lattice. Paraxial simulations confirm the rule: a circular Gaussian input develops a stable, topologically quantized $\ell=+q$ vortex in the reversed helicity, with $83\%$ conversion over three Rayleigh ranges and no fine-tuning. We propose a polarization-resolved photonic-lattice discriminator in which the slope of the measured OAM versus the independently written texture charge, one for torsion, two for birefringence, separates the two mechanisms.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors demonstrate that the surfaces of g-wave altermagnets can be engineered to exhibit d-wave altermagnetism, enabling a measurable spin-splitter effect (SSE) absent in the bulk. Using the Kubo formalism on a minimal slab model, they show this surface enhancement is constructive and linked to induced weak ferromagnetism, suggesting thin-film engineering as a viable route for functionalizing such materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical mechanism for enhancing magnetic functionalities (SSE) in topological/magnetic materials by exploiting boundary effects, which is highly relevant for designing next-generation spintronic devices.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To realize and study the spin-splitter effect (SSE) in altermagnets (AMs), overcoming the difficulty of finding metallic d-wave AMs at ambient conditions.

**Main result.** The surfaces of a g-wave altermagnet slab induce d-wave altermagnetism, leading to a finite SSE that is absent in the bulk. This surface response can be engineered via thin-film methods.

**Method.** The Kubo formalism is applied using a minimal single-orbital tight-binding model to compute spin conductivity and characterize the SSE angle.

**Model / system.** The study uses a minimal slab model based on a g-wave altermagnet, which incorporates hopping terms ($t_{1,k}, t_{2,k}, t_{3,k}, t_{AM,k}$) and spin-orbit coupling (SOC) terms. The system is analyzed in the context of surface effects.

**Key observables.** Spin conductivity ($\sigma_{S_z, yz}$), SSE angle ($	heta_{aa}$), weak ferromagnetism ($M_y$), and d-wave spin splitting in the electronic spectrum.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The maximum spin-splitter angle reached was up to 15 degrees. The analysis depends on the magnetic multipolar character of the AM order parameter.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The SSE is fundamentally linked to the magnetic multipolar character of the AM OP, and the calculations rely on a minimal slab model approximation.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the surface d-wave splitting enabling SSE (absent in bulk), plot $\sigma_{S_z, yz}$ vs. chemical potential for varying film thicknesses, and show layer-resolved weak ferromagnetism ($M_y$).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical platform (g-wave AM surfaces) and theoretical framework (Kubo formalism). It then calculates the SSE, demonstrating its surface origin via thickness dependence. Finally, it links this effect to induced weak ferromagnetism, suggesting material engineering strategies.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate surfaces of a $g$-wave altermagnet(AM) and show that they provide a platform for realizing $d$-wave altermagnetism and the associated spin-splitter functionality. Using the Kubo formalism applied to a minimal slab model, we evaluate the spin-splitter effect(SSE) by computing the spin conductivity corresponding to a transverse spin current induced by a longitudinal electric field. We find a finite SSE, absent in the bulk, that emerges from surface-induced $d$-wave altermagnetism. Strikingly, the sign pattern of the $d$-wave altermagnetism on both surfaces of the slab geometry is identical to each other, leading to additive contributions to SSE from the two surfaces, with a spin-splitter angle reaching up to 15 degrees. In addition, this response is intrinsically linked to an accompanying surface-induced weak ferromagnetism, which potentially enables control of altermagnetic domains via an external magnetic field and provides a route to optimize the SSE functionality. These results can be understood in terms of a bulk-boundary correspondence between surface states and bulk altermagnetic order parameters, where the magnetic multipolar character of the latter plays a central role. Our findings strongly suggest thin-film engineering as a viable strategy to functionalize non-$d$-wave AMs.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the challenge of applying bulk-boundary correspondence to complex nonlinear quantum systems. By developing an auxiliary system formalism, the authors successfully classify topological phases in 2D and demonstrate how stacking a 2D model into 3D can engineer distinct hybrid-order topological states, including third-order phases.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work extends topological concepts from linear systems into nonlinear regimes using a robust mathematical framework, which is highly relevant for understanding exotic phenomena in photonics and condensed matter wave physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The bulk-boundary correspondence (BBC) is poorly understood for nonlinear systems, especially those with multigap topologies, making topological description difficult.

**Main result.** The authors establish a multiband bulk-boundary correspondence and demonstrate that stacking engineering can realize exotic 3D hybrid-order topological phases (first-, second-, and third-order).

**Method.** They develop an auxiliary-system formalism to map the nonlinear eigenvalue problem onto a formally linear pencil matrix, allowing for topological classification.

**Model / system.** The study uses a two-dimensional (2D) spinless square-lattice model with two degrees of freedom per unit cell, which is then generalized to 3D via uniform or dimerized stacking along the third dimension.

**Key observables.** Topological invariants include the Chern number ($C_1$) and the mirror-graded winding number ($W_2$); boundary states are diagnosed by gapless modes ($\lambda=0$) and localized using the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Stacking parameters, such as $	ext{t}_1$ vs. $	ext{t}_2$ for dimerized stacking, determine the resulting order of the topological phase.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method relies on mapping the nonlinear problem to a formally linear auxiliary system ($P(\omega)$) and addresses multiple-gap topologies beyond previous single-gap studies.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the eigenvalue spectra under Open Boundary Conditions (OBC) showing coexisting first-order ($\omega=0$) and second-order ($\omega=-M-1$) boundary states, and analyze the auxiliary system spectrum to confirm topological invariants in 2D and 3D.

**Paper structure.** The paper first addresses the theoretical gap regarding nonlinear BBC using an auxiliary system formalism. It then analyzes the 2D case showing coexisting boundary/corner states, before extending the analysis to 3D stacking configurations (uniform vs. dimerized) to realize higher-order phases.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The bulk-boundary correspondence (BBC), which relates topological invariants to boundary modes, is well understood for linear systems but remains an open question in the presence of nonlinearity, where multigap topologies make the BBC obscure and the topological description troublesome. We address this by developing an auxiliary-system formalism that enables topological classification of nonlinear-eigenvalue systems. In the two-dimension (2D) case, we show that two fixed eigenvalues can harbor first-order gapless boundary modes and second-order corner modes. Stacking this 2D system along the third dimension (3D) reveals distinct hybrid-order realizations. Under uniform stacking, the corner states in the $xy$ plane transform into hinge states along the $z$ axis, yielding a 3D second-order phase, while the gapless boundary states become side-surface states, yielding a 3D first-order phase. For dimerized stacking, these states are further confined to the two ends of the $z$ axis, yielding a 3D third-order phase, and localized at the hinges, yielding a 3D second-order phase. Our results establish a multiband bulk-boundary correspondence and identify stacking engineering as a versatile platform for exploring hybrid-order topological phases in nonlinear systems.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper addresses systematic optical distortions that limit the precise placement of quantum emitters in nanophotonic circuits. By developing an *in situ* calibration protocol based on a Zernike vector-field model, the authors correct these field-dependent aberrations using patterned reference arrays. This correction significantly improves positioning accuracy and enhances the performance metrics of deterministic device fabrication.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides an essential metrology tool for quantum optics experiments, bridging the gap between statistical measurement precision and absolute positional accuracy required for scalable integrated quantum devices.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The ultimate yield of integrating quantum emitters into nanophotonic circuits is limited by uncorrected systematic optical distortions in cryogenic microscopy setups, despite achieving high statistical localization precision.

**Main result.** An *in situ* calibration protocol using a Zernike vector-field model successfully reduces residual systematic bias to 5.3 nm and improves the polarization registration accuracy of fabricated structures by 49%.

**Method.** The authors developed an in situ calibration protocol that models field-dependent optical distortions using a Zernike polynomial expansion, which is then applied to correct measured emitter positions.

**Model / system.** The system involves quantum emitters (semiconductor QDs) localized via microscopy and calibrated against lithographically defined gold nanodisk arrays within a custom cryogenic optical setup. The distortion correction relies on fitting the observed positional offsets to a Zernike vector-field model.

**Key observables.** Residual systematic bias (reduced to 5.3 nm), variance in emission polarization, localization repeatability ($\sim 4-6$ nm).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Cryogenic temperature (4 K), nanometer-scale accuracy requirement, Zernike polynomial order ($n=10$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The systematic optical distortions can be accurately modeled by a linear combination of Zernike polynomials; the calibration reference patterns are sufficient to characterize the field aberrations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the optical setup, SEM images of gold nanodisk arrays used for calibration, and performance evaluation comparing localization uncertainties before and after applying the Zernike distortion correction.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the limitation posed by systematic distortions. It then details the methodology using a Zernike model calibrated on reference patterns (nanodisks). Finally, it demonstrates the utility of this corrected positioning in improving deterministic fabrication metrics like polarization variance.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum photonic technologies greatly benefit from quantum light emitters with high brightness, indistinguishability, and reliable polarization characteristics. Achieving optimal performance relies on the accurate localization of emitters and their deterministic integration into tailored photonic structures with nanometer-scale accuracy. Although marker-based photoluminescence imaging techniques can achieve statistical fitting uncertainties below 10 nm, the ultimate integration yield is often limited by uncorrected systematic distortions in custom cryo-optical setups that compromise metrological accuracy. Here, we present an in situ calibration protocol that uses lithographically defined gold nanodisk arrays as references to calibrate optical distortions with a Zernike vector-field model. On held-out validation patterns beyond the calibration dataset, this correction reduces the residual systematic bias to 5.3 nm with a 2D scatter of 24.6 nm across the analyzed field of view. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying this correction to the deterministic fabrication of circular mesa structures around semiconductor quantum dots reduces the variance in emission polarization by 49%, indicating improved registration accuracy. This calibration strategy offers a practical route to high-yield deterministic integration of quantum emitters into scalable quantum photonic circuits.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores the complex electronic behavior of a quasi-one dimensional ladder lattice subjected to quasiperiodic modulation. The authors demonstrate a reentrant transition between localized and delocalized states, characterized by mobility edges. Furthermore, they identify robust edge modes whose existence is mapped onto an intriguing 'Quantum Butterfly' spectrum.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides detailed diagnostics—combining spectral measures (IPR), transport dynamics ($\mu$), and geometric features (butterfly)—to map out complex phase transitions in quasiperiodic systems, which is highly relevant for understanding localization phenomena beyond simple disorder models.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates a reentrant localization transition, quantum butterfly pattern, and robust edge modes in an aperiodic zig-zag ladder structure.

**Main result.** The system exhibits a re-emerging delocalization phase controlled by kinetic parameters, confirmed by mobility edges, alongside the observation of stable edge states resistant to moderate disorder.

**Method.** Analysis involves calculating spectral properties using Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR), studying transport dynamics via Mean Square Displacement (MSD), and mapping energy spectra onto a quantum butterfly structure.

**Model / system.** The model is a quasi-one dimensional zig-zag ladder network governed by a tight-binding Hamiltonian incorporating a quasiperiodic Aubry-Andre Harper (AAH) modulation in the long-range hopping integral.

**Key observables.** Inverse Participation Ratio ($	ext{IPR}_n$), Normalized Participation Ratio ($	ext{NPR}_n$), Mean Square Displacement (MSD), Edge Probability ($P_{	ext{edge}}$), and Transport Exponent ($\mu$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Slowness exponent ($\alpha$), hopping strengths ($t, \lambda_0$), disorder strength ($W_d$), and modulation frequency ($eta$ set to the golden mean).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that multifractal methods are applicable to characterize the energy landscape in this quasiperiodic model.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate IPR intensity plots showing re-entrant transitions, phase diagrams mapping delocalized/localized regimes ($\eta$), MSD curves characterizing transport exponents ($\mu$), and probability density maps distinguishing edge vs. bulk states on the quantum butterfly spectrum.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes localization diagnostics (IPR, $	ext{NPR}$) to find a re-entrant transition controlled by $\alpha$. It then uses dynamical studies (MSD) for confirmation, explores multifractality and the 'Quantum Butterfly' structure, and finally isolates robust edge modes using edge probability analysis.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Low dimensional tight-binding lattices in presence of quasiperiodic disorder generally exhibits localization transition. The system supports diffusive modes upto a limiting strength of disorder and all the eigenstates become localized beyond that critical strength thereby quenching the kinetic signature of the wavepacket. However, moving away from this situation, we demonstrate that with minimal long-range off-diagonal modulation, the eigenspectrum again may offer delocalization of electronic states for some subtle combination of kinetic parameters of the Hamiltonian leading to a second quantum phase change. The localization transitions are associated with the obvious presence of single-particle mobility edges. Multifractal energy landscape also shows quantum butterfly pattern with the in-gap robust edge modes. The re-emerging localization transition is manifested through the evaluation of inverse participation ratio, eigenspectrum and a pertinent quantum dynamical study.

</details>

**Summary.** The researchers demonstrated that Platinum nanoislands on TiO2 can act as highly efficient visible-light photocatalysts, contrary to previous beliefs. By using advanced microscopy, they quantified the photoactivity of Pt compared to Au, finding superior performance for discrete Pt structures. This work reclassifies Pt from a passive co-catalyst to an active component in metal-semiconductor hybrid devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state electrochemistry, the work involves quantifying charge carrier generation and separation efficiency under optical excitation, which touches upon open quantum systems concepts related to energy dissipation and interfacial coupling.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To challenge the assumption that noble metal catalysts like Platinum (Pt) are only passive co-catalysts with poor visible-light quantum efficiency in photoelectrochemical junctions.

**Main result.** Discrete Pt nanoislands exhibit robust, broadband visible-light photoactivity, showing an EQE-per-atom significantly higher than Au at specific wavelengths, suggesting they function as active light-responsive components.

**Method.** Quantitative scanning photoelectrochemical microscopy (SPECM) was used to measure wavelength-resolved external quantum efficiency (EQE), complemented by theoretical hot-carrier generation rate calculations.

**Model / system.** The study investigates metal-semiconductor junctions, specifically Au and Pt nanoislands deposited on a TiO2 support. The photoactivity is governed by the efficient separation of photogenerated carriers across the Schottky junction barrier.

**Key observables.** Wavelength-resolved external quantum efficiency (EQE), local extinction spectra, and the comparison of $	ext{Pt}$ vs. $	ext{Au}$ photoactivity as a function of nanostructure connectivity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The effective Schottky barriers ($\Phi_B$) for Au-TiO2 (1.1 eV) and Pt-TiO2 (1.3 eV); the comparison between discrete vs. connected nanoisland morphologies.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The measured signal reflects net interfacial charge separation; theoretical models provide an upper limit for carrier generation, neglecting certain recombination pathways.

**Figures summary.** Figures likely show position-resolved maps of EQE across Au and Pt arrays, correlating photoactivity with the local optical properties (LSPR vs. broadband absorption).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem by reviewing existing assumptions about noble metals; it presents experimental measurements using SPECM to quantify visible-light activity; theoretical modeling is used to interpret the results based on hot-carrier dynamics and barrier filtering.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Metal-semiconductor junctions in optoelectronic devices are commonly engineered to promote charge separation. In Pt/TiO2 Schottky junctions, Pt is typically regarded as a catalytic electron sink rather than a visible-light-active component. Here, we demonstrate that Pt nanoislands on TiO2 can generate photochemically active carriers under visible light excitation. Using quantitative scanning photoelectrochemical microscopy, we measure the wavelength-resolved external quantum efficiency (EQE) of Au and Pt nanoisland arrays on TiO2, and correlate their reactivity with their morphology and extinction spectra. Discrete 10 nm Pt nanoislands exhibit robust broadband visible light photoactivity - exceeding the photoactivity of similar-sized Au nanoislands under blue-green excitation - whereas Pt's photoactivity is strongly suppressed when the nanoislands are connected. Surprisingly, Pt exhibits an EQE-per-atom approx. 20 times higher than Au at 455 nm and approx. 2 times higher at 595 nm (at Au's optimum). We show an approximately wavelength-independent Pt internal quantum efficiency of approx. 1 percent across the visible spectral region. These findings reposition catalytic metals with strongly damped optical response in the visible as light-responsive components in metal-semiconductor hybrids, challenging the prevailing perception that they function solely as passive co-catalysts in photocatalytic systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores the intertwined physics of Charge Density Waves (CDW) and Superconductivity (SC) in graphene under strong magnetic fields. By analyzing transport measurements, the authors provide evidence that CDW order is responsible for stabilizing SC phases deep within the quantum Hall regime. This highlights a complex interplay between charge ordering, superconductivity, and Landau quantization in strongly correlated electron systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The observation that CDW order can stabilize superconductivity in a quantum Hall regime is highly relevant to understanding unconventional pairing mechanisms and competing orders in strongly correlated materials, which are central topics in condensed matter theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the complex interplay between Charge Density Wave (CDW) order, Superconductivity (SC), and Quantum Hall Effects (QHE) in a highly tunable electronic system.

**Main result.** The research demonstrates that CDW order is crucial for stabilizing superconductivity deep within the quantum Hall regime, marking an observation of SC coexisting with QHE signatures. The CDW and SC phases emerge from the same manifold of strongly mixed Landau levels.

**Method.** Transport measurements ($ho_{xx}, \sigma_{xy}$) are performed as functions of carrier density ($n$), perpendicular magnetic field ($B_\perp$), and displacement field ($D$). Temperature dependence studies reveal first-order phase transitions.

**Model / system.** The physical platform is rhombohedral hexalayer graphene (R6G) subjected to a large displacement field and a strong magnetic field. The system's low-energy spectrum features strongly mixed Landau levels due to flat band edges, enabling the investigation of correlated electronic phases.

**Key observables.** Integer Quantum Hall plateaus deviating from filling factors; pronounced thermal hysteresis (CDW signature); simultaneous vanishing of $ho_{xx}$ and $ho_{xy}$ (SC signature).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Strong perpendicular magnetic fields ($B_\perp > 2$ T); operating near the flat-band edge; temperature dependence across multiple Kelvin scales.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on mapping transport responses to diagnose distinct electronic orders (CDW, SC, QHE) coexisting in a strongly correlated electron liquid.

**Figures summary.** Figures map out phase boundaries in $n-D$ and $n-B_\perp$ space, showing regimes characterized by CDW signatures (hysteresis, re-entrant QHE) adjacent to superconducting pockets.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically maps the phase diagram of R6G under varying fields and doping, identifying distinct electronic phases (Regimes I, II, III). It then analyzes specific transport diagnostics—such as thermal hysteresis for CDW melting or simultaneous zero resistance for SC—to confirm the coexistence region.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Charge density wave (CDW) and superconductivity are both common in strongly interacting electron systems. While CDW order is ubiquitous in both quantum Hall systems and unconventional superconductors, superconductivity is generally suppressed by the strong magnetic fields required for Landau quantization. Here we investigate the intertwined CDW and superconducting phases of rhombohedral hexalayer graphene (R6G) in a large displacement field, which generates tunable flat band edges, and a strong magnetic field, which generates a manifold of nearly degenerate Landau levels. CDW order is accompanied by pronounced thermal hysteresis as expected for first-order melting transitions. Surprisingly, we find a series of strong integer quantum Hall effects at magnetic fields above ~2T with Hall conductance quantum numbers that deviate strongly from nearby integer filling factors, an observation that can be explained only by CDW order that mixes many Landau levels. We also find a nearby superconducting phase that is stabilized by perpendicular magnetic fields and persists deep within the quantum Hall regime. The CDW and superconducting phases develop on comparable temperature scales and emerge from the same manifold of strongly mixed Landau levels. These observations provide new insight into the interplay between superconductivity and CDW order in R6G at zero magnetic field.

</details>

**Summary.** This work reports the observation of a robust Nonlinear Hall Effect (NLHE) in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers. By measuring second-harmonic voltages and performing theoretical calculations, the authors prove that this effect originates from the intrinsic Berry curvature dipole generated at interfaces. This establishes these scalable thin films as a promising new platform for next-generation nonlinear spintronic devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter spintronics, the reliance on quantum geometric effects like the BCD and symmetry analysis mirrors concepts used in topological materials research relevant to AMO physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to observe and characterize the Nonlinear Hall Effect (NLHE) in technologically relevant magnetic multilayer platforms, extending its understanding beyond van der Waals crystals.

**Main result.** A robust NLHE was observed in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers, confirming that the effect is driven by the intrinsic Berry curvature dipole (BCD), establishing these films as a new platform for spintronic applications.

**Method.** The research combines transport measurements of second-harmonic transverse voltage ($V_{xy}^{2\omega}$) with theoretical analysis using first-principles DFT calculations to confirm the underlying electronic mechanism.

**Model / system.** The system is a polycrystalline magnetic multilayer heterostructure, specifically $	ext{Ta}/	ext{Pt}/[	ext{Ir}/	ext{Fe}/	ext{Co}/	ext{Pt}]_5/	ext{Pt}$. The physics is governed by spin-orbit coupling and broken structural inversion symmetry at the interfaces.

**Key observables.** Second-harmonic transverse voltage ($V_{xy}^{2\omega}$), which shows quadratic dependence on current, frequency independence, and magnetic field independence; also measured $R_{xx}$, $V_{xy}^{1\omega}$, and XRD patterns.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature range (2 K to room temperature); applied magnetic fields ($\pm 2 	ext{ T}$); multilayer periodicity ($[\dots]_5$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The observed NLHE signal is assumed to be dominated by the intrinsic Berry curvature dipole mechanism, supported by vanishing third-harmonic response and scaling analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figures show layer architecture, Hall bar geometry, $R_{xx}$ vs. T (metallic behavior), XRD patterns confirming texture, linear transport measurements ($V^{1\omega}$), and nonlinear measurements ($V^{2\omega}$) showing quadratic dependence on current.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the measurement setup by measuring linear transport; it then measures the second-harmonic voltage to confirm a genuine nonlinear response; finally, theoretical analysis (DFT) links this observed signal magnitude directly to the intrinsic Berry curvature dipole component ($D_{yz}$).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The Nonlinear Hall effect(NLHE) driven principally by the Berry curvature dipole has been established in non-centrosymmetric vander Waals crystals, topological semimetals, and moiré superlattices, but its extension to technologically mature heavy-metal/ferromagnet multilayer platforms remains largely unexplored. Here, we report the observation of a robust NLHE in polycrystalline magnetic multilayers, persisting from 2 K to room temperature. The second-harmonic transverse voltage is independent of both excitation frequency and applied out-of-plane magnetic field, while the vanishingly small third-harmonic response confirms that the observed signal is not dominated by a quantum-metric contribution and instead reflects a genuine second-order electronic response. A scaling analysis of the second-order Hall conductivity against the longitudinal conductivity identifies a dominant, conductivity-independent term establishing the intrinsic berry curvature dipole. Our theoretical analysis, supported by first-principles DFT calculations, further satisfies and corroborates the experimental results. These results establish sputter-deposited polycrystalline thin film as the first engineered magnetic multilayer platform for BCD-driven nonlinear Hall transport, extending the NLHE material landscape beyond van der Waals systems into scalable, industry-compatible thin-film spintronic architectures suitable for high frequency rectifications and nonlinear sensors.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper presents a theoretical design to create multiple Majorana zero modes (MZMs) by coupling chiral hinge states from a higher-order topological insulator (HOTI) with an s-wave superconductor. By reducing the system dimensionality, opposite hinge states form helical channels, and superconducting pairing opens a gap, localizing four robust MZMs at the corners of the sample.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, material-agnostic theoretical blueprint for engineering multiple MZMs using established superconducting techniques on advanced topological materials, bridging HOTI physics with superconductivity.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work proposes a theoretical route to realize spatially separated Majorana zero modes (MZMs) by exploiting the boundary physics of higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs). This is achieved through proximity coupling with an s-wave superconductor in a quasi-two-dimensional geometry.

**Main result.** The model successfully predicts the formation of four localized MZMs at the corners, characterizing the system as a second-order topological superconductor. These corner modes are shown to be robust against weak to moderate disorder.

**Method.** The study employs theoretical modeling using the Bogoliubov-de-Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian and analyzes spectral properties under varying boundary conditions and disorder strengths.

**Model / system.** The system is a chiral HOTI, which hosts gapless hinge states in 3D. By confining it quasi-2D, opposite chiral hinge states hybridize into helical channels. Superconducting proximity effect induces effective p-wave pairing on these channels, leading to the topological superconducting state.

**Key observables.** Zero-bias conductance peaks (STM signature), localized MZMs at corners, and the spectral gap opening in the BdG spectrum.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The confinement direction ($x$), the chemical potential ($\mu$) tuned into reconstructed hinge bands, and the superconducting pairing strength ($\Delta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the chiral HOTI can be realized and that the proximity effect induces effective p-wave pairing. Robustness is confirmed only against weak-to-moderate disorder.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate gapless hinge states in 3D, the formation of helical channels upon confinement, and BdG spectra showing the emergence of four localized MZMs at the corners when tuned into the topological superconducting phase.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from identifying gapless hinge states in a 3D HOTI to analyzing their hybridization in a quasi-2D geometry. The core mechanism involves proximity coupling inducing p-wave pairing, which opens a topological gap and localizes MZMs at the boundaries (corners). Disorder robustness is confirmed last.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Majorana zero modes (MZMs) in topological superconductors have attracted broad research interest for their potential applications in topological quantum computation. In this work, we propose a quasi-two-dimensional route to realize spatially separated MZMs in a chiral higher-order topological insulator (HOTI) proximitized by a conventional $s$-wave superconductor through a theoretical model study. In three dimensions, the chiral HOTI hosts gapless hinge states along the $z$ direction, arising from a mass term that anisotropically gaps the surface Dirac cones of a topological insulator. By confining the sample along the $x$ direction while keeping it extended along $y$ and finite along $z$, opposite $z$-directed chiral hinge states hybridize and effectively form one-dimensional helical channels. Incorporating the superconducting proximity effect into this quasi-two-dimensional system induces effective $p$-wave pairing in these helical channels, thereby opening a topological gap. A fully open-boundary sample then hosts four localized MZMs, one at each endpoint of the helical channels, realizing a second-order topological superconductor characterized by Majorana corner modes. In addition to MZMs, we also find that superconducting pairing in this model produces extended Majorana hinge modes in three dimensions. Furthermore, representative disorder calculations indicate that these Majorana corner modes are robust against weak-to-moderate disorder, provided the excitation gap remains open. These results establish finite-size-coupled chiral hinge states as a promising platform for engineering multiple MZMs via conventional superconducting proximity effect.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes an effective, singularity-free model for black hole interiors using a scalar field description that results in three distinct layers: a core, a transition layer, and a crust. It treats the entire process of black hole formation and evaporation as a quasi-static thermodynamic cycle driven by negative energy within the core. The analysis relies heavily on solving Einstein equations and applying advanced concepts from statistical mechanics to describe matter states.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on GR/BH physics, the core concept of modeling BH evaporation as a quasi-static, adiabatic thermodynamic engine—where negative energy acts as the working substance—draws strong parallels to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics treatments of open quantum systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To construct an effective, singularity-free model for the interior of a black hole by treating its structure as a thermodynamic system.

**Main result.** The black hole interior is modeled as a three-layered structure (core, transition layer, crust) whose evolution mimics a quasi-static, almost adiabatic thermodynamic engine cycle.

**Method.** Solving static Einstein equations and applying WKB approximations to derive the energy-momentum tensor components for the various matter layers.

**Model / system.** The model uses an effective scalar field with non-linear self-interaction potential to describe a three-layer black hole interior: a negative energy AdS core, a transition layer, and a positive-energy quasi-particle crust.

**Key observables.** Metric functions, mass functions $m(r)$, energy densities ($ho$), pressures ($p_r, p_\perp$), and the active Komar mass $M_{	ext{Komar}}(r)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Negative inverse temperature parameter ($eta$) governing the core condensate; quasi-particle density; Schwarzschild radius $2GM_{	ext{ADM}}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system is treated as a static problem initially, and the process of formation/evaporation is modeled as an almost adiabatic thermodynamic cycle.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the radial ordering of the three layers ($R_- < R^+ < R_S$) and show the scalar self-interaction potential $V(\phi)$ across these regions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by defining the physical system, deriving components using WKB approximations for the crust (leading to an isotropic EoS), analyzing stability near the null-gravity transition layer ($R^+$) via test particle motion, and finally framing the entire structure within a thermodynamic cycle analogy.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose an effective, singularity-free model of the black hole interior described entirely by a scalar field with a non-linear self-interaction potential. The interior consists of three layers -- a core, a transition layer, and a crust -- each fixed by the local quasi-particle density and the corresponding extremum of the potential of the field. The crust is a layer of massive, positive-energy thermal excitations above the zero-potential well, beneath a genuine Schwarzschild horizon at $r = 2GM_{\rm ADM}$. The core is an AdS-type region of negative energy density, it simulates a condensate of quasi-particles which carry zero classical kinetic energy and form a negative potential well governed by a negative inverse temperature parameter. The two regions are joined through Israel matching across the transition layer, which sits at an approximately null-gravity hypersurface of maximal regular matter density and where both the sign of the energy density and the type of thermal excitations change. Solving the static Einstein equations, we obtain the metric and mass functions of each layer, the edge equation of state of the crust, the linear stability condition of the null-gravity surface for ordinary and effectively negative mass matter, and the two-temperature thermodynamics linking the kinetic excitations to the negative temperature ground state. The framework unifies core and crust within a single field description and highlights the role of the negative energy AdS core and the associated negative temperature notion in describing black hole interior. In this picture the formation and Hawking evaporation of a black hole appear as a quasi-static cycle of an almost adiabatic thermodynamic engine, with the negative energy core as the working substance.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study proposes a dipole-engineered Janus MgAlB2 monolayer as a superior anode material for Li-ion batteries. By breaking structural symmetry, the material generates an intrinsic polarization that significantly lowers the lithium diffusion barrier and increases storage capacity compared to its symmetric counterparts. The work establishes intrinsic polarization as a powerful design principle for next-generation energy materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state electrochemistry, the concept of engineering an intrinsic electric field via structural asymmetry (Janus effect) to control charge transport kinetics is analogous to designing quantum interfaces or controlling local potentials in AMO systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research addresses the need for novel, high-performance anode materials for Li-ion batteries that overcome the capacity limitations of conventional anodes.

**Main result.** The dipole-engineered Janus MgAlB2 monolayer exhibits exceptional performance, achieving a high theoretical specific capacity (1470.24 mAh/g) with ultrafast Li ion transport due to its intrinsic polarization.

**Method.** First-principles calculations using DFT were employed to model the electronic structure, electrochemical properties, and ion diffusion kinetics of the proposed material.

**Model / system.** The system is a Janus MgAlB2 monolayer, engineered by breaking the symmetry of parent MBenes structures (Mg2B2 or Al2B2) through Al substitution. This asymmetry generates a permanent out-of-plane polarization and built-in electric field.

**Key observables.** Low Li diffusion barrier (17.1 meV), high theoretical specific capacity (1470.24 mAh/g), dipole moment, and intrinsic polarization magnitude.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Room-temperature diffusion coefficient ($3.43	imes10^{-10} 	ext{ cm}^2/	ext{s}$), volume expansion ($\le 3.7\%$), and the built-in electric field strength.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations assume that intrinsic polarization can be utilized as a design parameter to regulate both the thermodynamics (storage capacity) and kinetics (ion transport) of lithium storage.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate optimized geometries, electronic structure analysis (PDOS/Band Structure), charge transfer mapping (EDD plots), and calculated diffusion pathways/barriers for Li ion movement.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by identifying the limitations of symmetric MBenes, proposing the Janus structure to induce polarization, and then using DFT calculations to quantify how this intrinsic dipole enhances Li adsorption capacity and accelerates ion diffusion compared to pristine materials.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we propose a group II/IIIA-based Janus MBene, MgAlB_2, and investigate its electrochemical properties using first-principles calculations. The substitution of one Mg layer in Mg_2B_2 MBene by an Al layer breaks the structural symmetry and generates a permanent out-of-plane polarization, giving rise to a distinct electronic environment compared with the parent Mg_2B_2 and Al_2B_2 monolayers. Electronic-structure analysis reveals enhanced orbital hybridization among B, Mg, and Al states near the Fermi level, resulting in improved electronic delocalization across the monolayer. The Janus MgAlB_2 monolayer is found to possess excellent dynamical, mechanical, and thermal stability. Owing to its polarization-modified energy landscape, Li ions migrate with an exceptionally low diffusion barrier of 17.1 meV, corresponding to a room-temperature diffusion coefficient of 3.43x10^-10 cm^2/s. Unlike the pristine Mg_2B_2 and Al_2B_2 monolayers, which support only a single stable adsorption layer, MgAlB_2 accommodates two complete Li layers. Detailed analysis shows that the residual polarization retained after first-layer lithiation continues to promote Li adsorption, whereas increasing Li-Li electrostatic interactions eventually limit further storage. As a result, the Janus monolayer delivers a high theoretical specific capacity of 1470.24 mAh/g together with a small volume expansion of only 3.7% during maximum lithiation. The present study demonstrates that intrinsic polarization can be utilized to regulate both the thermodynamics and kinetics of Li storage, providing a design strategy for high-rate and high-capacity two-dimensional electrode materials.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors perform advanced correlated-electron calculations on pentacene oligomers to characterize triplet-triplet multiexciton states. They demonstrate that these states are not localized pairs but rather delocalized quantum superpositions of multiple configurations. This theoretical finding resolves discrepancies regarding intramolecular triplet diffusion and suggests alternative pathways for energy dissipation in polymeric materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the complex many-body dynamics in organic semiconductors, providing a detailed electronic structure explanation for excited state behavior that goes beyond simple localized models, which is crucial for understanding energy transfer mechanisms relevant to quantum optics and materials science.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to determine the true nature of triplet-triplet multiexciton states in polypentacene oligomers: whether they are localized nearest-neighbor pairs or delocalized quantum superpositions.

**Main result.** The eigenstates are found to be complex quantum superpositions involving all accessible intertriplet separations, which explains the observed lack of simple intramolecular triplet diffusion.

**Method.** Correlated-electron calculations using the Pariser-Parr-Pople (PPP) Hamiltonian solved via Multiple Reference Singles and Doubles Configuration Interaction (MRSDCI).

**Model / system.** The system models are three- and four-unit pentacene oligomers, serving as microscopic representations for polypentacene. The calculations utilize a molecular exciton basis that explicitly separates Frenkel, charge-transfer, and triplet-pair configurations.

**Key observables.** Energy levels of $1(T_1T_1)$ eigenstates, absorption spectra (ESAs), and transient absorption (TA) features, particularly the signal at 710 nm.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The calculations fix parameters like the onsite Hubbard repulsion U = 6.7 eV and use a molecular exciton basis derived from frontier MOs.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Key limitations include the exclusion of electron-vibration interactions and the reliance on the semiempirical PPP Hamiltonian.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically contrast localized vs. delocalized models for eigenstates, show the $4	ext{Pc}$ structure, and illustrate intermonomer Charge Transfer (CT) channels responsible for observed ESA peaks.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops by first establishing the theoretical framework using MRSDCI on PPP Hamiltonian; it then calculates and analyzes the resulting multiexciton eigenstates, comparing these predictions against experimental TA measurements to deduce the physical nature of triplet interactions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present correlated-electron calculations of optical spin-singlet and triplet-triplet multiexciton states in three- and four-unit pentacene oligomers as microscopic models for polypentacene. The calculations use the Pariser-Parr-Pople Hamiltonian, multiple-reference singles and doubles configuration interaction, and a molecular exciton basis that resolves Frenkel, charge-transfer, and triplet-pair (T1T1) configurations in real space. We find that the complete set of 1(T1T1) eigenstates lies in a narrow, nearly degenerate energy window near the lowest optical exciton and that no eigenstate can be identified with a single localized triplet-pair configuration. Instead, each triplet-pair eigenstate is a quantum superposition of configurations containing all accessible intertriplet separations. This electronic structure explains the perceived absence of intramolecular triplet diffusion in pentacene oligomers, polypentacene, and polytetracene solutions, while leaving open the possibility of intermolecular singlet fission in films with appreciable interchain interactions.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates the temperature dependence and physical origins of channel noise in InP HEMTs used in critical applications like radio astronomy. By measuring noise from 4 K to 300 K, the authors determined that excess noise is dominated by impact ionization and real-space transfer effects, not just simple shot noise. The results guide material optimization by identifying the optimal indium composition (60%) for minimum noise performance.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on semiconductor device physics rather than fundamental quantum dynamics, understanding noise sources at cryogenic temperatures is crucial for building sensitive quantum measurement devices (like superconducting qubits or detectors) that rely on low-noise amplifiers.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to fully characterize the various physical mechanisms responsible for noise generation in InP HEMTs with $\mathrm{In_{x}Ga_{1-x}As}$ channels across a wide temperature range (4 K to 300 K).

**Main result.** The excess channel noise at cryogenic temperatures is attributed not only to shot noise but also significantly to impact ionization and real-space transfer noise. The 60% indium content exhibited the lowest overall channel noise.

**Method.** Noise was quantified by extracting the equivalent drain noise temperature ($T_d$) using both on-wafer measurements ($\geq 40$ K) and Low Noise Amplifier (LNA)-based cryogenic measurements ($4 	ext{ K} - 40 	ext{ K}$).

**Model / system.** The physical system is a 100-nm gate-length InP HEMT utilizing an $\mathrm{In_{x}Ga_{1-x}As}$ channel, tested with varying indium contents ($x=53\%, 60\%, 70\%$). The noise analysis decomposes the total current noise into thermal and excess components.

**Key observables.** Equivalent drain noise temperature ($T_d$), channel current noise spectral density ($\mathrm{S}_{id}$), and the excess noise term ($\mathrm{S}_{id,ex}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature range (4 K to 300 K); Channel indium content ($x$); Bias conditions ($V_{ds} = 0.5 	ext{ V}, I_d = 5 	ext{ mA}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the total noise can be separated into thermal and excess components, allowing for the identification of temperature-dependent and independent noise sources.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate $T_d$ vs. ambient temperature comparing on-wafer and LNA data; $\mathrm{S}_{id}$ at 4 K versus indium content ($x$), demonstrating the minimum excess noise at $x=60\%$.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically measures channel noise across temperatures, decomposes the total noise into thermal and excess parts, analyzes the temperature dependence of these components, and finally attributes the residual excess noise to specific hot-electron effects like impact ionization and RST noise.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The InP high-electron-mobility transistor (HEMT) is indispensable for low-noise amplifiers (LNAs) in radio astronomy and quantum computing. The composition of the $\mathrm{In_{x}Ga_{1-x}As}$ channel in InP HEMT is known to influence the LNA noise performance. However, the various physical mechanisms responsible for noise generation are not fully characterized and understood. Here, we investigate the $\mathrm{In_{x}Ga_{1-x}As}$ channel noise from 4 K to 300 K for 100-nm gate-length InP HEMTs with channel indium content of 53\%, 60\% and 70\%. Channel noise was quantified by extracting the equivalent drain noise temperature $\mathit{T}_{d}$ using both on-wafer and LNA-based measurements, covering 40-300 K and 4-40 K, respectively. The 60\% indium channel InP HEMT exhibited the lowest channel noise across the full temperature range. The $\mathit{T}_{d}$ extracted from on-wafer characterization was found to obey a parabolic temperature dependence which predicted the $\mathit{T}_{d}$ at 4 K for all InP HEMTs in good agreement with LNA-based measurements. By expressing the channel noise as the sum of one thermal and one excess noise term, it was found that the former increased linearly with ambient temperature and dominated at 300 K. The channel noise at 4 K was determined by the excess noise term and exhibited a non-monotonic dependence on the channel indium content in the InP HEMT. The results suggest that the excess noise in the InP HEMT originates not only from temperature-independent shot noise but also from impact ionization and real-space transfer noise.

</details>

**Summary.** This work introduces Quantum Geometric Friedel Oscillations (QGFOs), which arise from the nontrivial quantum geometry inherent in flat bands. Unlike conventional oscillations that vanish at high temperatures, QGFOs persist robustly because their decay length is set by a temperature-independent 'quantum metric length.' Measuring these unique oscillations offers a powerful tool to probe the underlying geometric structure of electronic band theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter transport, the concept of geometric protection leading to robust, temperature-independent signatures is highly relevant for understanding coherence in quantum devices or mesoscopic systems where thermal decoherence is a major concern.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The conventional theory of Friedel oscillations is incomplete when considering Bloch wavefunctions with nontrivial quantum geometry, necessitating the identification of a new oscillation type.

**Main result.** Quantum Geometric Friedel Oscillations (QGFOs) exist due to the quantum metric in flat bands; these oscillations persist robustly at high temperatures where conventional oscillations are washed out.

**Method.** The analysis involves deriving and comparing susceptibility functions, separating contributions into conventional and quantum geometric parts ($\chi_f = \chi^c_f + \chi^g_f$).

**Model / system.** The study focuses on metals exhibiting isolated (nearly) flat bands at the Fermi energy, modeled using tight-binding Hamiltonians in 1D and 2D settings.

**Key observables.** Oscillation periods ($2k_F$ vs. $q_G$), decay lengths ($\xi_T$ vs. $\ell_{QM}$), and the normalized LDOS variation $\deltaho_{	ext{norm}}(q)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$), Fermi momentum ($k_F$), flat-band bandwidth ($W_f$), and quantum metric length ($\ell_{QM}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often relies on approximations like the Born approximation or high-temperature limits to isolate the geometric contributions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematic band structures, real-space density modulations showing coexistence/persistence of oscillations, and Fourier spectra highlighting distinct peaks at $2k_F$ and $q_G$.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds by first identifying the theoretical incompleteness of conventional theory, then deriving the QGFO susceptibility ($\chi^g$), demonstrating its unique temperature dependence (persistence), and finally quantifying its spatial extent ($\Omega_{	ext{QGFOs}}$) relative to topological invariants.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In conventional Friedel oscillations, the real-space charge density oscillations induced by an impurity are characterized by an oscillation period set by the Fermi momentum. In this work, we show that the conventional theory is incomplete when the Bloch wavefunctions carry nontrivial quantum geometry. We demonstrate that in metals with an isolated (nearly) flat band at the Fermi energy, quantum geometry induces a distinct type of oscillations, which we call the \emph{quantum geometric Friedel oscillations} (QGFOs). The period of the QGFOs is set by the momentum space separation of the quantum metric hot spots of the flat band. The conventional and quantum metric-induced oscillations coexist at low temperatures. At higher temperatures, the conventional Friedel oscillations away from the impurity site are set by the thermal length such that the oscillations can be easily washed out by temperature effects. Remarkably, the QGFOs decay length is set by the quantum metric length which is defined by the integration of the quantum metric of the flat band. As a result, the QGFOs can persist even at temperatures much larger than the bandwidth of the flat band. Moreover, the decay length is independent of temperature for a wide range of temperatures which is a manifestation of the quantum metric protection. In conclusion, we show that the quantum metric induces novel Friedel oscillations. Our work suggests that the measurement of the QGFOs is a powerful way to detect the quantum metric length (which is associated with the integral of the quantum metric) and the quantum metric hot spot separations (which are associated with the distribution of the quantum metric in the momentum space).

</details>
